The squad-mates are concerned because the patient has been talking nonsensically and will not answer their questions appropriately. Rectal temperature shows 104.4°F. You immediately begin implementing cooling measures and place the patient in water immersion. At what temperature do you remove the patient from the water immersion?

questions.solution: Correct Option D - 101.5°F - 102.0°F: High heat and humidity can impair the body's ability to dissipate heat through evaporation, convection, conduction, and radiation. Exertional heat illness is the result of an inability to maintain adequate cardiac output because of strenuous physical exercise and environmental heat stress. Rapid cooling is the most effective strategy to prevent ongoing morbidity and mortality. When the rectal temperature reaches 101 to 102 degrees F, active cooling measures should be stopped. Ice water immersion is the ideal method of cooling, but tepid water will be helpful if cold water is unavailable. If a rectal temperature is not available, then the patient should be cooled until he begins to shiver. A typical rate of cooling with cold water immersion is 0.37 degrees F per minute. Incorrect Options: Option A, B and C - Active cooling should stop when the patient begins to shiver or the patient's temperature reaches 101.5 to 102 degrees Fahrenheit. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.solution: Correct Option B - Apply erythromycin eye ointment to the eye to slowly loosen the glue and then gently pry open the lid. Bacitracin ointment or mineral oil can be applied to the fingers for the same purpose. Have him follow up with ophthalmology in a day to make sure all the glue is gone from his eye: Cyanoacylate (Crazy or Super Glue) is also used in surgical wound adhesives. It is nontoxic, however, it can cause problems by sticking together lips, fingers, or eyelids. To remove the glue, an oil-based material is needed such as erythromycin or Bacitracin ointment or mineral oil . For eyes that are stuck together, erythromycin eye ointment is effective and very safe - this applies to glue stuck to the cornea as well as the lids. Follow-up with an eye doctor can be done in a day or two. Incorrect Options: Option A - The boy should be immediately sent to the ophthalmologist's office for surgical debridement: This option suggests sending the child directly to an ophthalmologist for surgical debridement. Surgical debridement involves removing tissue that may have been damaged or glued together by the cyanoacrylate glue. While surgical debridement may be necessary in some cases of severe eye injury, it is not typically the first-line approach for a child who accidentally gets Super Glue in their eye. Surgical interventions should be considered only if less invasive methods are unsuccessful or if there is evidence of significant eye damage. In this case, it's important to start with less invasive and less risky measures. Option C - Irrigate the eye with warm water and soak the stuck fingers in Betadine to loosen the glue: This option suggests irrigating the eye with warm water and soaking the glued fingers in Betadine to loosen the glue. While irrigation may be appropriate for some chemical exposures, it may not be the best approach for cyanoacrylate glue, as this type of glue hardens upon exposure to water. Irrigating the eye in this case could potentially worsen the situation and create further complications. It is not recommended to use water or Betadine to address cyanoacrylate glue in the eye or on the skin. Option D - Gently pry open the eyelid and fingers with traction: This option suggests attempting to gently pry open the eyelid and fingers with traction. This approach is not recommended, especially when dealing with a child's eye. Attempting to forcibly open the eyelid can cause damage to the delicate eye structures, and prying open glued fingers could result in injury as well. This approach may lead to more harm than good and should be avoided. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A 5-year-old boy presents with right knee pain and a limp. He has no history of trauma. His hip is abducted and externally rotated,with exacerbation of pain with internal rotation. What is the most likely cause of this symptom?
questions.stemHtml: A 5-year-old boy presents with right knee pain and a limp. He has no history of trauma. His hip is abducted and externally rotated,with exacerbation of pain  with internal rotation. What is the most likely cause of this symptom?
questions.solution: Correct Option C- Transient synovitis: Transient synovitis and septic arthritis are the most common causes of atraumatic hip pain in children . Transient synovitis usually occurs in children between the ages of 3 and 8 years of age, most often in boys. Children typically have had symptoms for one to three days at presentation and will demonstrate an antalgic gait with an abducted and externally rotated hip at rest. Pain is exacerbated with internal rotation of the hip, although pain with motion is less severe than in children with septic arthritis of the hip. Referred pain to the knee may be the only complaint , so careful inspection of the hip is mandatory in all patients with isolated knee pain. Referred pain from the hip to knee is usually a dull pain that is located anteriorly and does not localize to bone or soft tissue. Examination of the knee is usually normal. The hip exam typically demonstrates a limited range of motion with pain. Serious causes of hip pain must be excluded, including septic arthritis, fracture, slipped capital femoral epiphysis (SCFE), and Legg-Calve-Perthes disease. Patients with transient synovitis rarely have a fever Management of transient synovitis is purely supportive and includes rest and NSAIDs. Incorrect Options: Option A- Femoral neck fracture: Hip fracture in a paediatric patient is suggested by high-force trauma, and severe tenderness is common. Option B- Osteogenesis imperfecta: Osteogenesis imperfecta is a rare disease that causes problems in bone synthesis due to collagen defects. Frequent fractures are common, and a physical examination may demonstrate blue sclerae, deafness, and ligamentous laxity. Subclinical cases may be more common than previously recognized. Option D- Slipped capital femoral epiphysis (SCFE): SCFE occurs when the femoral epiphysis slips off the metaphysis, usually in adolescents. @Neet_pg_bot

Schizophrenia is not associated with elevated blood pressure and elevated heart rate. Option C- Thyrotoxicosis: Thyrotoxicosis is a possibility however less likely as there would not be memory change in this condition. Option D- Overdose of barbiturates: Barbiturate overdose would present with respiratory depression, not tachycardia. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A family brings their two-year-old child into the pediatrician’s OPD for a “white glow” that they noticed in their child’s left eye over the past two months. The child is otherwise healthy. Family history is unremarkable. There is no history of trauma. On exam, there is an orange red reflection in the child’s right pupil. There is a white reflection from the left pupil. The first mutation leading to this patient’s condition most likely occurred in which of the following?
questions.stemHtml:
A family brings their two-year-old child into the pediatrician’s OPD for a “white glow” that they noticed in their child’s left eye over the past two months. The child is otherwise healthy. Family history is unremarkable. There is no history of trauma. On exam, there is an orange red reflection in the child’s right pupil. There is a white reflection from the left pupil.
The first mutation leading to this patient’s condition most likely occurred in which of the following?
questions.solution: Correct Option B - The child’s somatic cell: Retinoblastoma is high on the differential for a child presenting with leukocoria (abnormal white reflex). In most cases unilateral retinoblastoma is not genetically inherited. Two active copies of the retinoblastoma gene ( RB1 ) are present in cells. The first mutation occurs in either a somatic or a germline cell . The second mutation only occurs in somatic cells (known as the “two hit” hypothesis). Both must be mutated for the clinical manifestations of retinoblastoma to develop. Bilateral retinoblastoma (bilateral leukocoria) frequently suggests a germline mutation, or a mutation in all cells. Patients with this hereditary germline form are also at risk for other cancers, such as pineoblastoma, soft tissue sarcomas, and melanoma. Incorrect Options: Option A - RB enzyme: RB is a tumor suppressor gene. It encodes for a protein that inhibits progression of the cell cycle until a cell is ready to divide. Option C - Mitochondrial DNA: Retinoblastoma is not a mitochondrial disease. Examples of mitochondrial diseases are Kearns-Sayre syndrome, myoclonus epilepsy with ragged-red fibers, and mitochondrial encephalomyopathy with lactic acidosis and stroke-like episodes (MELAS syndrome). Option D - Diploid zygote: The vignette most likely refers to a somatic mutation (not germline) and therefore this mutation would not be expected to be found in the diploid zygote (fusion of two gametes). @Neet_pg_bot

  • The first mutation occurs in either a somatic or a germline cell. The second mutation only occurs in somatic cells (known as the “two hit” hypothesis).
  • Both must be mutated for the clinical manifestations of retinoblastoma to develop.
  • Bilateral retinoblastoma (bilateral leukocoria) frequently suggests a germline mutation, or a mutation in all cells. Patients with this hereditary germline form are also at risk for other cancers, such as pineoblastoma, soft tissue sarcomas, and melanoma.

Incorrect Options:

Option A - RB enzyme: RB is a tumor suppressor gene. It encodes for a protein that inhibits progression of the cell cycle until a cell is ready to divide.

Option C - Mitochondrial DNA: Retinoblastoma is not a mitochondrial disease. Examples of mitochondrial diseases are Kearns-Sayre syndrome, myoclonus epilepsy with ragged-red fibers, and mitochondrial encephalomyopathy with lactic acidosis and stroke-like episodes (MELAS syndrome).

Option D - Diploid zygote: The vignette most likely refers to a somatic mutation (not germline) and therefore this mutation would not be expected to be found in the diploid zygote (fusion of two gametes).

questions.answerText: Place towels under the right side of the board
questions.solution: Correct Option C - Place towels under the right side of the board: " Supine hypotensive syndrome " is caused by mechanical obstruction of venous return in the gravid uterus. questions.stem: Which of the following theories of aging in geriatric medicine suggests that aging is primarily driven by the accumulation of DNA damage and mutations over time?
questions.stemHtml: Which of the following theories of aging in geriatric medicine suggests that aging is primarily driven by the accumulation of DNA damage and mutations over time?
questions.solution: Correct Option A - Free Radical Theory: This theory posits that aging is mainly a result of the cumulative damage caused by reactive oxygen species (free radicals) on cellular structures, particularly DNA. Over time, this damage can lead to mutations and other cellular changes associated with aging. Incorrect Options: Option B - Wear and Tear Theory: This theory suggests that aging is a result of the body wearing out over time due to repeated use and environmental stress. While this theory has some validity, it does not focus on DNA damage and mutations as the primary drivers of aging. Option C - Programmed Aging Theory: The Programmed Aging Theory proposes that aging is genetically programmed and follows a predetermined pattern. This theory implies that aging is not solely a result of DNA damage and mutations, making it an incorrect choice for this question. Option D - Hormonal Theory: The Hormonal Theory of aging posits that changes in hormone levels play a significant role in the aging process. It emphasizes the role of hormones such as insulin, growth hormone, and sex hormones. While hormonal changes are associated with aging, they are not primarily linked to DNA damage and mutations, making this option incorrect. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: What was/were the chemotherapy agents used in the adjuvant chemotherapy arm of GOG 122 (Randall et al JCO 2006), the phase III trial of stage III or IV endometrial carcinoma?
questions.stemHtml: What was/were the chemotherapy agents used in the adjuvant chemotherapy arm of GOG 122 (Randall et al JCO 2006), the phase III trial of stage III or IV endometrial carcinoma?
questions.solution: Correct Option D - Cisplatin and Doxorubicin: GOG 122 sought to compare the efficacy of adjuvant whole-abdominal irradiation versus adjuvant chemotherapy for locally advanced, optimally debulked endometrial cancer, which had previously never been compared in a prospective, randomized trial. The study enrolled 422 patients with stage III or IV endometrial carcinoma of any histology who had undergone total abdominal hysterectomy, bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy, and optimal debulking with less than 2 cm of residual gross disease remaining at any one site. Lymph node sampling was optional. Following surgery, patients were randomized to: Adjuvant whole-abdominal radiation Adjuvant chemotherapy (chemotherapy was doxorubicin (60 mg/m 2 ) and cisplatin (50 mg/m2), administered every 3 weeks for 7 total cycles, followed by 1 additional cycle of cisplatin alone. The maximum allowable cumulative dose of doxorubicin was 420 mg/m 2 ). The primary endpoint of the study was progression-free survival, with overall survival as a secondary endpoint. At a median follow-up of 74 months: 5-year progression-free survival was 38% for the whole-abdominal irradiation arm vs. 50% for the chemotherapy arm (p=0.007). 5-year overall survival was 42% for the whole-abdominal irradiation arm vs. 55% for the chemotherapy arm (p=0.004). The patients receiving chemotherapy experienced more grade 3-4 hematologic and gastrointestinal toxicity, as compared with the patients receiving whole-abdominal irradiation. The study authors concluded that chemotherapy improved progression-free survival and overall survival as compared to whole-abdominal irradiation. This trial played a role in establishing the role of adjuvant chemotherapy for patients with advanced or high-risk disease. However, please note that the NCCN Guidelines recommends a regimen of carboplatin and taxol for non-sarcoma endometrial cancers (or Carboplatin, Taxol, and Herceptin for HER2-positive uterine serous carcinomas). Incorrect Options: Option A - Carboplatin: Carboplatin is a platinum-based chemotherapy agent, but it was not used in the adjuvant chemotherapy arm of GOG 122. Therefore, this option is not correct. Option B - Carboplatin and Paclitaxel: While this combination is commonly used in various gynecological malignancies, including endometrial carcinoma, it was not the chemotherapy regimen used in the adjuvant chemotherapy arm of GOG 122. This option is not correct for this specific trial. Option C - Cisplatin: Cisplatin is a platinum-based chemotherapy agent, and it was indeed used in the adjuvant chemotherapy arm of GOG 122. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stemHtml: A 28-year-old male who presented with mild chest pain, cough, and the subjective feeling of shortness of breath was evaluated, and found to have an anterior mediastinal mass with no additional lesion concerns for metastatic spread in his CT thorax. His AFP level was normal and beta-hCG level was 488 IU/L. Based on the patient's clinical presentation, which of the following treatments would you recommend?
questions.solution: Correct Option D - Chemotherapy +/- surgery: Based on the clinical information above, his presentation is most consistent with a mediastinal seminoma without evidence of metastatic spread. Mediastinal germ cell tumour are generally managed with chemotherapy followed by surgical resection. Mediastinal seminoma without metastases is considered Good-Risk and chemotherapy consists of 3 cycles of bleomycin, cisplatin, and etoposide (BEP) or 4 cycles of EP chemotherapy. Like testicular and CNS seminoma, mediastinal seminomas are quite sensitive to chemotherapy and thus surgery is generally considered for residual disease after chemotherapy. Note that not all cases of residual disease after chemotherapy should have surgery, and the management of residual mass after chemotherapy is controversial. These patients should be managed in a multidisciplinary setting. Using this treatment paradigm the long term overall survival rate is excellent. For patients that are unable to tolerate chemotherapy, radiation therapy can be considered, as seminomas are also responsive to radiation. Note that all mediastinal non-seminoma germ cell tumors (NSGCT) are Poor-Risk and should be treated with 4 cycles of BEP or 4 cycles of VIP (Etoposide, Ifosfamide plus Mesna, and Cisplatin). Incorrect Options: Option A - Surgery alone: Surgery alone is not recommended in this case. While surgery might be an option for localized testicular tumors, an anterior mediastinal mass with elevated serum markers suggests a non-seminomatous germ cell tumor (NSGCT), which is more aggressive and usually requires a multimodal approach involving chemotherapy and potentially surgery. Option B - Surgery + adjuvant chemotherapy: This option could be considered, but it's important to note that chemotherapy is typically administered before surgery in the management of NSGCT. Chemotherapy helps to shrink the tumor and treat any potential microscopic spread of the disease. Option C - Surgery + adjuvant radiation: Radiation therapy is not typically used as the primary treatment for non-seminomatous germ cell tumors. Chemotherapy is the mainstay of treatment, and radiation might be considered in specific cases, usually after surgery, for residual masses that are resistant to chemotherapy. @Neet_pg_bot

Biopsy reveals a likely melanoma but further staining is needed. Which of the following stains is more specific to melanoma than other primary sites of disease?
questions.solution: Correct Option B - S100: S100 is a protein that is found in cells of neural crest origin, and it is expressed in melanocytes, which are the cells that give rise to melanoma. Immunohistochemical staining for S100 is a valuable diagnostic tool in identifying melanoma cells. It is particularly useful for confirming the diagnosis of melanoma when the histological features alone are not definitive. S100 staining is considered specific for melanoma and neuroectodermal tumors, as it is not typically expressed in most other primary malignancies. Therefore, when S100 staining is positive in a tumor biopsy, it strongly supports the diagnosis of melanoma. Incorrect Options: Option A - P63 / P40: P63 and P40 are markers commonly used to identify squamous cell carcinomas and are not specific to melanoma. They are often used to differentiate between different types of carcinomas, especially in cases where the histological appearance alone is insufficient for diagnosis. Option C - AE1/AE3: AE1 and AE3 are cytokeratin antibodies that are used to identify epithelial cells. They are not specific to melanoma and are typically used to differentiate epithelial tumors from other types of tumors. Option D - OCT3/4: OCT3/4 is an immunohistochemical marker used to detect germ cell tumors, particularly in the testes and ovaries. It is not specific to melanoma and is unrelated to the diagnosis of melanoma. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.solution: Correct Option C - Aplastic anaemia: Paroxysmal nocturnal haemoglobinuria (PNH) is an unusual condition with patients typically presenting in their 30s. The genetic underpinning of this condition is an acquired somatic mutation of the PIGA gene (Phosphatidylinositol Glycan class A) on the X chromosome. The protein product of the PIGA gene is involved in the creation of the glycosylphosphatidylinositol (GPI) anchor which serves to attach cell surface proteins to the cell membrane. Without the GPI anchor for protein attachment, these cells are prone to both intravascular haemolysis (lack of CD59) and extravascular haemolysis (lack of CD55). Clinical symptoms typically include erectile dysfunction, abdominal pain, (these smooth muscle symptoms are thought to be secondary to a decreased amount of nitric oxide caused by free haemoglobin during haemolysis) profound fatigue, and haematuria (see intravascular haemolysis above) especially during night-time hours. Thrombosis (large abdominal vein) is common in this patient population as free haemoglobin is associated with a pro-thrombotic milieu. Laboratory abnormalities include: high levels of LDH, low levels of haptoglobin, unbound haemoglobin in the urine, anaemia, reticulocytosis, with a negative direct ant globin test (Coombs test). The diagnosis can be confirmed using flow cytometry. PNH and aplastic anaemia are often found in tandem (this occurs in greater than 50% of cases). Although not completely understood, the underlying mechanism appears to be immune escape by PNH cells and subsequent proliferation in the setting on aplastic anaemia Incorrect Options: Option A - Chronic myeloid leukaemia (CML): CML is a type of cancer that starts in certain blood-forming cells of the bone marrow. It is characterized by a specific genetic abnormality in the cancer cells, the Philadelphia chromosome. CML would not explain the absence of CD55 and CD59 as seen in PNH. Option B - Myelodysplastic syndrome (MDS): MDS refers to a group of diverse bone marrow disorders in which the bone marrow does not produce enough healthy blood cells. While MDS might cause anaemia and other blood-related symptoms, the absence of CD55 and CD59, as well as the patient's overall clinical picture, are more consistent with PNH than with MDS. Option D - Fanconi's anaemia: Fanconi's anaemia is a rare inherited bone marrow failure syndrome that is characterized by physical abnormalities, bone marrow failure, and a higher risk of cancer. The genetic basis and clinical presentation differ from those of PNH. questions.stem: A 52-year-old woman was seen in haematology clinic due to elevated ferritin. She was recently diagnosed with hypothyroidism and has been taking levothyroxine regularly. She had menopause at the age of 45. No family history of hemochromatosis. She is otherwise asymptomatic without any signs of cirrhosis liver or congestive heart failure. Laboratory studies are summarized below. CBC: WBC 6,000/uL, Hb- 14.7 g/dL, MCV 88 FL, platelet count 200,000/uL. BMP: Normal Random Blood Glucose: 90 mg/dL LFT: Normal. Iron studies: ferritin 975 ng/mL, serum iron 234 ug/dL, iron binding capacity 265 ug/dL and transferrin saturation 60%. HFE genotyping revealed a homozygous C282Y genotype. What treatment option would you recommend?
questions.stemHtml:
A 52-year-old woman was seen in haematology clinic due to elevated ferritin. She was recently diagnosed with hypothyroidism and has been taking levothyroxine regularly. She had menopause at the age of 45. No family history of hemochromatosis. She is otherwise asymptomatic without any signs of cirrhosis liver or congestive heart failure. Laboratory studies are summarized below.
CBC: WBC 6,000/uL, Hb- 14.7 g/dL, MCV 88 FL, platelet count 200,000/uL.
BMP: Normal
Random Blood Glucose: 90 mg/dL
LFT: Normal.
Iron studies: ferritin 975 ng/mL, serum iron 234 ug/dL, iron binding capacity 265 ug/dL and transferrin saturation 60%.
HFE genotyping revealed a homozygous C282Y genotype.
What treatment option would you recommend?

options.label: B
options.text: Hepatic MRI to determine liver iron content

questions.solution: Correct Option D - Weekly phlebotomy: Hereditary hemochromatosis is a genetic disorder characterized by systemic iron overload. The major HFE mutation is C282Y, and approximately 15% of individuals of the northern European origin are heterozygotes and 0.5% are homozygotes. C282Y heterozygotes do not develop disease. Approximately two-thirds of homozygotes for C282Y develop iron overload with elevated ferritin and markedly high transferrin saturation. Other HFE mutations are H63D and S65C. Compound heterozygotes (C282Y/H63D) may also develop hemochromatosis, but far less likely. The effect of S65C mutation is very minimal. HFE hemochromatosis is generally diagnosed in fifth or sixth decade of life (in women after menopause). Clinical symptoms include fatigue, loss of libido, abdominal pain and arthralgia. Cirrhosis of the liver, cardiomyopathy, diabetes and endocrine dysfunction are frequent due organ damage from iron accumulation. The fully penetrant form of the disease (bronze diabetes) is rarely seen. Treatment of HFE hemochromatosis in C282Y homozygotes is weekly phlebotomy to remove accumulated iron. Removal of 500 ml of blood removes approximately 200 mg iron. Phlebotomy is recommended in individuals with iron overload even in the absence of end organ damage. The goal is to reduce the ferritin to <100 ng/mL. Incorrect Options: Option A - Observation: This option is not recommended for hereditary hemochromatosis with elevated ferritin levels. Left untreated, hereditary hemochromatosis can lead to iron overload, which may result in various complications such as liver cirrhosis, diabetes, and heart problems. Active intervention is necessary to manage iron levels. Option B - Hepatic MRI to determine liver iron content: While MRI can be used to estimate liver iron content, it is not the first-line treatment for hereditary hemochromatosis. MRI can help monitor iron overload and guide treatment decisions, but it is not the primary therapeutic approach. Option C - Oral deferasirox: Deferasirox is an iron chelator that can be used to manage iron overload. However, in cases of hereditary hemochromatosis, especially with high ferritin levels, phlebotomy (removing blood to lower iron levels) is generally the preferred initial treatment. Deferasirox might be considered in specific cases where phlebotomy is not feasible or well-tolerated @Neet_pg_bot

His medical history is insignificant, except for excessive bleeding from the umbilical stump after birth, frequent nosebleeds, and easy bruising. Fibrin, fibrinogen, PT and aPTT are normal. However, a clot solubility assay using 2% acetic acid results in clot dissolution. What is the likely diagnosis?

However, a clot solubility assay using 2% acetic acid results in clot dissolution. What is the likely diagnosis?
questions.solution: Correct Option D- Factor XIII deficiency: Factor XIII is a coagulation factor responsible for stabilizing blood clots by cross-linking fibrin. A deficiency in Factor XIII can lead to impaired clot stability. The excessive bleeding from the umbilical stump after birth, frequent nosebleeds, easy bruising, and a recent intracranial bleed and hematoma following a fall, is characteristic of a bleeding disorder. The clot solubility assay using 2% acetic acid results in clot dissolution, which is a specific test for Factor XIII deficiency. In Factor XIII deficiency, clots are formed but lack the stability provided by cross-linking, making them susceptible to dissolution in acetic acid. Incorrect Options: Option A- Deficiency of fibrinogen: Fibrinogen is involved in the early stages of blood clot formation, and its deficiency typically results in prolonged PT and aPTT. In this case, both PT and aPTT are normal, making fibrinogen deficiency less likely. Option B- Factor V deficiency: Factor V is also involved in the coagulation cascade, and its deficiency would typically result in prolonged PT and aPTT. Normal PT and aPTT make Factor V deficiency less likely. Option C- Factor VIII deficiency: Factor VIII deficiency is known as hemophilia A and is characterized by prolonged aPTT. In this case, aPTT is reported as normal, making Factor VIII deficiency less likely. @Neet_pg_bot

An FNAC of the neck mass was consistent with a necrotic lymph node and a surgical excisional biopsy of the cervical lymph node revealed complete effacement of normal lymph node architecture by a nodular infiltrate composed of large malignant appearing lymphoid cells. questions.solution: Correct Option B- Dexamethasone, methotrexate, ifosfamide, pegaspargase, and etoposide (often referred to as the SMILE regimen): This regimen is L-asparaginase based, which is favored for patients with advanced stage ENK/T lymphomas. L-asparaginase is a cornerstone drug for this particular type of lymphoma due to its efficacy against cells with high levels of P-glycoprotein expression, a common feature of ENK/T cells. Typical anthracycline containing regimens used in other aggressive lymphomas have proven inferior in treating ENK/T lymphomas, potentially explained by high levels of P-glycoprotein expression (Yamaguchi M, et al. Cancer. 1995) on the lymphoma cells. L-asparaginase based regimens are favored for patients with advanced stage disease. Incorrect Options: Option A- Rituximab and CODOX-M alternating with R-IVAC: Rituximab is an anti-CD20 monoclonal antibody. The patient’s immunophenotype is CD20-, meaning the cells do not express CD20, so rituximab would be ineffective. questions.solution: Correct Option D - Transfusion Related Acute Lung Injury (TRALI): Transfusion-related acute lung injury (TRALI) is a serious complication that can occur following blood product transfusion, typically within 6 hours after the transfusion. TRALI is characterized by sudden onset acute respiratory distress, hypoxia (low blood oxygen levels), and bilateral pulmonary infiltrates on imaging. Other symptoms may include fever, cyanosis, and hypotension. The clinical presentation in this case aligns with TRALI: The patient developed dyspnea and cyanosis within a few hours after receiving packed red blood cell transfusion. The physical exam findings, including tachycardia, normal heart sounds, absence of increased JVP, and absence of peripheral edema, do not indicate cardiac-related issues like congestive heart failure. Bilateral pulmonary infiltrates on CXR suggest acute respiratory distress. The leukocyte count of 7800/μL may be a response to the acute lung injury. Incorrect Options: Option A - Febrile Non-Hemolytic Transfusion Reaction (FNHTR): FNHTR is characterized by fever and chills during or shortly after a transfusion, without severe respiratory symptoms or evidence of lung injury. The patient in this case has severe respiratory distress and bilateral pulmonary infiltrates, which are not typical of FNHTR. Option B - Sepsis: While sepsis can cause fever, tachycardia, and hypotension, it typically presents with other systemic signs of infection, and the acute respiratory distress with pulmonary infiltrates seen on CXR is not a typical presentation of sepsis alone. Option C - Transfusion Associated Circulatory Overload (TACO): TACO occurs due to rapid or excessive transfusion, leading to volume overload. It may cause symptoms of fluid overload such as elevated blood pressure, increased JVP, and peripheral edema. questions.solution: Correct Option A - Refers to the range of values which have the highest likelihood of containing the true value within a specific population: The confidence interval refers to the range of values which have the highest likelihood of containing the true value within a specific population based on concepts such as repeat sampling and analyzing the number of data points sampled and the variance. Incorrect Options: Option B - This confidence interval, by definition, must contain the true value: The confidence interval does not guarantee that it contains the true value of the parameter being estimated. Instead, it provides a range of values within which the true value is likely to fall with a certain level of confidence. The level of confidence is typically expressed as a percentage, such as 95% confidence interval, which means that there is a 95% likelihood that the true value lies within the interval. Option C - The variability of the data determines the width of the confidence interval: While variability is one factor that affects the width of the confidence interval, it is not the only factor. The width of the confidence interval also depends on the sample size and the chosen level of confidence. A larger sample size generally leads to a narrower confidence interval, as it provides more information about the population parameter being estimated. Option D - Confidence intervals with higher degrees of confidence must be narrower: Confidence intervals with higher degrees of confidence are wider, not narrower. When you want to be more confident that the interval contains the true value, you need to widen the interval. For example, a 95% confidence interval will be wider than a 90% confidence interval for the same data. This is because a higher confidence level requires a greater level of certainty and, therefore, a wider range of values to be included in the interval. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.solution: Correct Option A - Tiotropium: The antimuscarinic drug tiotropium treats asthma and chronic obstructive lung disease (COPD). This patient exhibits a persistent productive cough, a history of tobacco use, and greater anteroposterior lung girth coarse crackles on physical examination. All of these characteristics firmly point to a COPD diagnosis. Tiotropium specifically blocks the M3 muscarinic receptors in the airways, leading to the relaxation of bronchial smooth muscles and decreased bronchoconstriction. The competing binding of Tiotropium (and other long-acting parasympatholytics) to muscarinic receptors decreases the parasympathetic tone on the bronchioles, which prevents bronchoconstriction. Moreover, tiotropium also inhibits mucus secretion from goblet cells, leading to a reduction in airway obstruction. These results enhance lung efficacy and lessen the signs and symptoms of airway blockage. Incorrect Options: Option B - Fluticasone: Fluticasone and other inhaled glucocorticoids prevent the production of several cytokines, which has an anti-inflammatory impact. The transcription factor NF-B, which typically promotes the generation of inflammatory substances (such as TNF-), is inactivated by glucocorticoids in the nucleus. Despite being a component of the multimodal treatment for chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, inhaled glucocorticoids do not counteract the effects of vagal activation on the airways. Option C- Montelukast: Anti-inflammatory drugs called anti-leukotrienes, such as montelukast, inhibit leukotriene receptors. (CysLT1). Leukotrienes cause bronchoconstriction and lung hyperreactivity. As a result, leukotriene receptor blockade causes bronchodilation. Montelukast is not recommended to treat chronic obstructive pulmonary disease despite reducing lung irritation. This drug has been shown to lessen the frequency of severe asthma episodes and is frequently prescribed to manage asthma. Additionally, montelukast does not counter the impacts of vagal activation on the airways. Option D - Albuterol: Beta 2-agonist, albuterol causes bronchodilation right away. It is used to treat acute bouts of asthma and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease because it is a short-acting medication; it is not a component of long-term maintenance treatment. questions.answerText: Asthma is characterized by airway obstruction that is partially or completely reversible with treatment.
questions.solution: Correct Option A - Asthma is characterized by airway obstruction that is partially or completely reversible with treatment: Asthma is a reversible condition that affects the airways of the lungs. During an asthma attack or exacerbation, the airways become inflamed, narrowed, and produce excessive mucus, leading to symptoms such as coughing, wheezing, chest tightness, and shortness of breath. In most cases, the airway obstruction in asthma is reversible , either spontaneously or with appropriate treatment. The degree of reversibility can vary from person to person and can depend on factors such as the severity and duration of the asthma attack, the individual's age and overall health, and the effectiveness of the treatment. However, in some cases, repeated and severe asthma attacks can lead to irreversible lung damage and a decline in lung function, known as airway remodelling. Airway remodelling is characterized by structural changes in the airways, such as increased smooth muscle and collagen deposition, which can lead to persistent airflow limitation and reduced response to bronchodilators. This irreversible lung damage is more likely to occur in individuals with severe and uncontrolled asthma, particularly those who smoke or have other risk factors such as chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD).. Incorrect Options: Option B - Asthma is caused by irreversible damage to the airways, leading to permanent airway obstruction: Asthma is a reversible condition that can be managed with appropriate treatment. Irreversible damage to the airways can occur in other obstructive lung diseases like chronic bronchitis or emphysema. Option C - Asthma is caused by chronic bronchitis, leading to narrowing of the airways: Asthma and chronic bronchitis are two distinct diseases with different underlying pathophysiology. Chronic bronchitis is characterized by chronic inflammation and mucus production in the bronchi, leading to airway obstruction and impaired gas exchange. Option D - Asthma is caused by emphysema, leading to decreased lung elasticity: Asthma and emphysema are two distinct diseases with different underlying pathophysiology. On physical examination, the patient appears cachectic, and clubbing is noted. Auscultation of the chest reveals coarse crackles in both lungs. Laboratory investigations reveal leukocytosis and increased C-reactive protein (CRP) levels. Chest X-ray shows bronchial wall thickening and cystic changes in the lung fields. Which of the following diagnostic tests would be most appropriate for this patient?
questions.stemHtml:
A 35-year-old female patient has presented to the clinic with a chronic cough for the past 6 months. She reports producing copious amounts of sputum and complains of shortness of breath. She has had a history of recurrent respiratory tract infections since childhood. On physical examination, the patient appears cachectic, and clubbing is noted. Auscultation of the chest reveals coarse crackles in both lungs. Laboratory investigations reveal leukocytosis and increased C-reactive protein (CRP) levels. Chest X-ray shows bronchial wall thickening and cystic changes in the lung fields.
Which of the following diagnostic tests would be most appropriate for this patient?
questions.solution: Correct Option A - Chest Computed Tomography (CT) scan: The patient's clinical presentation and laboratory findings are consistent with Bronchiectasis, a chronic respiratory disease characterized by permanent dilatation and thickening of the bronchial walls. The most appropriate diagnostic test for Bronchiectasis is a chest computed tomography (CT) scan. A Chest Computed Tomography scan is the gold standard diagnostic test for Bronchiectasis. It is the most sensitive and specific test for diagnosing the condition and allows for accurate localization and characterization of bronchial abnormalities. Computed Tomography findings in Bronchiectasis include bronchial wall thickening, cystic changes, signet ring appearance on cross section, and bronchial dilation with visible airway lumen. Computed Tomography can also help identify the underlying cause of Bronchiectasis, such as cystic fibrosis, immune deficiencies, focal obstruction or allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis. Incorrect Options: Option B - Sputum culture and sensitivity: Sputum culture and sensitivity can help identify the causative organism in patients with Bronchiectasis. Sputum culture may be useful in guiding antibiotic therapy in patients with recurrent infections. However, sputum culture and sensitivity alone are not a definitive diagnostic test for Bronchiectasis. It can also be positive in other respiratory conditions, such as pneumonia or chronic obstructive pulmonary disease. Option C - Pulmonary Function Tests: Pulmonary Function Tests are non-invasive and typically involve a series of breathing tests, including spirometry, lung volume measurements, and diffusing capacity tests Pulmonary Function Tests are not diagnostic for Bronchiectasis, but they can help assess the disease's severity and monitor treatment response. Pulmonary Function Tests may reveal obstructive or restrictive lung patterns, reduced lung volumes, and decreased gas exchange. Option D - Bronchoscopy: During a bronchoscopy, a thin, flexible tube with a camera on its end is inserted through the nose or mouth and into the lungs. The camera allows the doctor to see the inside of the airways and to look for signs of inflammation, blockages, or abnormalities. Bronchoscopy may be useful in identifying endobronchial lesions, such as tumors or foreign bodies, which can cause Bronchiectasis. However, bronchoscopy is not routinely performed in the diagnostic workup of Bronchiectasis and is not the most appropriate initial diagnostic test. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stemHtml: A 75-year-old man presents to the pulmonology clinic with a complaint of difficulty to breath and coughing. The patient has a 40-pack-year smoking history. On examination, the patient has a pink appearance and is cachectic with obvious difficulty breathing with pursed lips. The post-bronchodilator FEV1/FVC ratio is 0.6. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.solution: Correct Option B - Emphysema COPD is the persistent airflow limitation caused by obstruction of smaller airways and limitation of airflow in which FEV1/FVC < 0.70 is characteristic. Emphysema is a type of COPD characterised by the loss of alveoli due to the destruction of alveolar walls and capillaries, which result in permanent dilatation of pulmonary airspaces. These patients are cachectic with a pink appearance because the partial pressure of oxygen is not much reduced. Incorrect Options: Option A - Asthma Asthma is a chronic respiratory inflammatory disease characterised by bronchial hypersensitivity and reversible airflow obstruction. Patients present with severe shortness of breath, cough and wheezing. It may be allergic asthma due to triggers such as atopy, pollen, domestic animals, mites, mould spores and floor dust. Non-allergic asthma is due to viral respiratory tract infection, cold air, exercise-induced asthma, stress, and aspirin-induced asthma. Option C - Chronic bronchitis Chronic bronchitis is a type of COPD characterised by chronic cough with expectoration for at least three months per year for two consecutive years. A productive cough is the hallmark of the disease rather than shortness of breath. Patients are obese and have central cyanosis due to hypoxia and may also have peripheral oedema. Therefore, these patients are called “blue bloaters.” Option D - Bronchiectasis Bronchiectasis is an abnormal and irreversible dilatation of the bronchial tree due to progressive obstruction of the airway and mucous plugging by repeated bronchial inflammation. It may be caused by cystic fibrosis or after severe pneumonia, primary ciliary dyskinesia, Kartagener syndrome and allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis, smoking and bronchial narrowing by COPD. Patients present with copious mucopurulent sputum, repeated rhinosinusitis, and blood in sputum. @Neet_pg_bot

Pulmonary function test shows no difference in FEV1 before and after inhaled short-term bronchodilator. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial treatment?

options.label: A

options.label: B
options.text: Avoid prescribing sympathomimetics due to lack of airway responsiveness

options.label: C

options.label: D
options.text: Prescribe a short acting bronchodilator for use as needed

questions.answerText: Prescribe a short acting bronchodilator for use as needed
questions.solution: Correct Option D - Prescribe a short acting bronchodilator for use as needed: Short-acting bronchodilators provide the best relief of symptoms in COPD and should be prescribed for all patients with minimal symptoms and low risk of exacerbation. Bronchodilators induce long-term improvements in symptoms, exercise capacity, and airflow limitation, even in patients who do not have spirometric improvement after a test dose. Incorrect Options: Option A - Introduce steroids to sensitize airway to sympathomimetics: This option is not appropriate as it suggests the use of steroids to sensitize the airways to sympathomimetics. Steroids are not used for this purpose in COPD management. Steroids have anti-inflammatory effects and are typically reserved for patients with severe COPD or those experiencing exacerbations. In this patient with minimally symptomatic COPD and no evidence of bronchodilator responsiveness on pulmonary function testing, starting steroids is not indicated. Option B - Avoid prescribing sympathomimetics due to lack of airway responsiveness: This option is also not appropriate as it suggests avoiding sympathomimetics based on the lack of airway responsiveness on pulmonary function testing. Short-acting bronchodilators (sympathomimetics) are the mainstay of treatment for relieving symptoms in COPD, regardless of the degree of airway responsiveness on testing. Many patients with COPD experience symptom relief and improved exercise capacity with short-acting bronchodilators, even if their FEV1 does not show significant improvement. Option C - Repeat the test after three months: Repeating the pulmonary function test after only three months is not necessary or indicated in this case. Pulmonary function testing is typically performed annually to monitor disease progression and response to treatment. In this patient with newly diagnosed minimally symptomatic COPD and low risk of exacerbation, the focus should be on symptom relief and appropriate management rather than frequent testing. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.solution: Correct Option A - Streptococcus pneumoniae: The patient presents with the clinical features of community-acquired pneumonia (CAP) Pneumonia tends to spread via droplets. Streptococcus pneumoniae is the most common cause of CAP. The likelihood that other organisms may be involved depends on the age of the patient and the clinical scenario (previous illness, immunocompromised state, travel history, exposure to animals or contaminated water). Patients usually present with fever, rigours, chills, cough productive of mucopurulent sputum, pleuritis chest pain, and upper abdominal pain. Physical examination reveals dull percussion note and bronchial breathing with crackles. Incorrect Options: Option B - Haemophilus influenzae: Haemophilus influenzae is more common in the elderly population. It is less commonly seen as an aetiological factor than Streptococcus pneumoniae. Option D - Legionella pneumophila: Legionella pneumophila is a cause of CAP in cases of local outbreaks centred on contaminated cooling towers in hotels, hospitals, and other industrial buildings. A pneumothorax can be either spontaneous or traumatic, and the severity can range from mild to life-threatening. The initial treatment for a pneumothorax is determined on its size and severity. A moderate to large pneumothorax is likely the cause of the patient's rapid onset chest discomfort and shortness of breath in this case. This diagnosis is also supported by the physical examination finding of diminished breath sounds on the left side. The appearance of a collapsed left lung on a chest X-ray confirms the diagnosis of a pneumothorax. The initial course of action is to insert a chest tube. In order to allow for the drainage of air and re-expansion of the lung, a tube is inserted into the pleural space in this procedure. Chest tube placement is the most effective and definitive treatment for a moderate to large pneumothorax. Incorrect Options: Option A - Needle Aspiration: Needle aspiration is a less invasive procedure than chest tube placement and can be used to treat a small pneumothorax. However, it is not appropriate for a moderate to large pneumothorax. Option C - Observation with supplemental oxygen: Observation with supplemental oxygen may be appropriate for a small pneumothorax that is not causing significant respiratory distress. However, in this case, the patient is experiencing significant symptoms and has a collapsed lung, which indicates the need for more aggressive management. Spirometry shows an obstructive pattern with a 15% increase in FEV1 after bronchodilator administration. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis in this patient?
questions.solution: Correct Option D - Occupational asthma: Occupational asthma is caused by exposure to substances at the workplace. These substances can trigger an immune response in the respiratory system, leading to inflammation and narrowing of the airways. Common agents associated with occupational asthma include flour and grain dust, wood dust, aldehydes, latex, and isocyanates. Clinical features of occupational asthma include the following: Cough, wheezing, chest tightness, and shortness of breath. These symptoms usually occur during work and may improve when the person is away from work or on vacation. Over time, if exposure to the agent continues, the symptoms may worsen and become persistent, even when the person is away from work. questions.stemHtml: A 45-year-old female with a history of hypertension presents to the emergency department with weakness and malaise. Laboratory testing reveals a serum potassium level of 2.5 mEq/L. Which of the following medications is the most likely cause of the patient's electrolyte imbalance?
questions.solution: Correct Option C: Hydrochlorothiazide Hydrochlorothiazide is a thiazide diuretic commonly used to treat hypertension. Thiazide diuretics increase renal excretion of sodium, chloride, and water, and can also cause potassium loss through increased urinary excretion. Thiazide diuretics reduce potassium concentration in blood through two indirect mechanisms: inhibition of sodium chloride symporter at distal convoluted tubule of a nephroand stimulation of aldosterone that activates Na+/K+-ATPase at collecting duct. Inhibition of sodium-chloride symporter increases availability of sodium and chloride in urine. When the urine reaches the collecting duct, the increase in sodium and chloride availability activates Na+/K+-ATPase, which increases the absorption of sodium and excretion of potassium into the urine. Long term administration of thiazide diuretics reduces total body blood volume. This activates the renin-angiotensin system, stimulates the secretion of aldosterone, thus activating Na+/K+-ATPase, increasing excretion of potassium in urine. Hypokalemia (low serum potassium level) is a potential adverse effect of hydrochlorothiazide and can lead to symptoms such as weakness, malaise, and muscle cramps. Incorrect options: Option A: Lisinopril Lisinopril is an angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitor commonly used to treat hypertension. ACE inhibitors can cause hyperkalemia (high serum potassium level) because it inhibits the formation of angiotensin II which activates the formation of aldosterone. Aldosterone directly increases potassium excretion. Thus, low aldosterone by ACE inhibitors cause potassium retention leading to hyperkalemia. In some patients, but this is not the likely cause of the patient's electrolyte imbalance in this scenario. Option B: Metoprolol Metoprolol is a beta-blocker commonly used to treat hypertension. Beta-blockers do not typically cause significant electrolyte imbalances , and hypokalemia is not a common adverse effect. Erectile dysfunction, cardiovascular (bradycardia, AV block, HF), CNS (seizures, sleep alterations), dyslipidemia (metoprolol), masked hypoglycemia, asthma/COPD exacerbations are the adverse effects of beta blockers. Option D: Amlodipine Amlodipine is a calcium channel blocker commonly used to treat hypertension. Calcium channel blockers do not typically cause significant electrolyte imbalances, and hypokalemia is not a common adverse effect. Which of the following drugs is commonly used in the treatment of CKD to reduce proteinuria?
questions.solution: Correct Option A: Lisinopril Lisinopril is an angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitor medication that is commonly used in the treatment of CKD. It acts by blocking the conversion of angiotensin I to angiotensin II. By inhibiting angiotensin II, lisinopril reduces aldosterone secretion and promotes sodium and water excretion, which can lead to hyperkalemia. Angiotensin II specifically constrict the efferent arteriole and increases the glomerular filtration pressure, and increases the proteinuria. One of the therapeutic effects of ACE inhibitors is reducing proteinuria by dilating the efferent arteriole and thus decreasing the filtration pressure, which ultimately leads to reduced proteinuria, which is a common complication of CKD. Incorrect options: Option B: Hydrochlorothiazide Hydrochlorothiazide is a thiazide diuretic medication that can help reduce blood pressure in patients with hypertension and CKD. It decreases sodium reabsorption and therefore decreases fluid reabsorption; this directly causes decreased levels of circulating sodium. It does not have a significant effect on reducing proteinuria. Option C: Amlodipine Amlodipine is a calcium channel blocker medication that can help reduce blood pressure in patients with hypertension and CKD. It does not have a significant effect on reducing proteinuria. Which of the following is the most likely mechanism by which insulin and dextrose will correct the patient's hyperkalemia?
questions.stemHtml: A 45-year-old male presents to the emergency department with weakness, nausea, and confusion. Lab results show severe hyperkalemia. The patient is prescribed insulin and dextrose. Which of the following is the most likely mechanism by which insulin and dextrose will correct the patient's hyperkalemia?
questions.solution: Correct Option B: Increased cellular uptake of potassium Insulin promotes the movement of potassium from the extracellular fluid to the intracellular fluid , where it is sequestered in cells such as skeletal muscle and liver. Insulin shifts potassium into cells by stimulating the activity of Na+-H+ antiporter on cell membrane, promoting the entry of sodium into cells, which leads to activation of the Na+-K+ ATPase, causing an electrogenic influx of potassium. IV insulin leads to a dose-dependent decline in serum potassium levels. Dextrose is given to prevent hypoglycemia that can be caused by insulin administration. The combination of insulin and dextrose results in increased cellular uptake of potassium and a decrease in serum potassium levels. This is the mechanism by which insulin and dextrose are used to treat hyperkalemia. Incorrect options: Option A: Increased renal excretion of potassium Certain medications, such as loop diuretics and potassium-sparing diuretics , increase the excretion of potassium by the kidneys However, insulin and dextrose do not directly affect renal potassium excretion and are not the primary mechanism by which they treat hyperkalemia. Option C: Decreased gastrointestinal absorption of potassium Certain medications, such as kayexalate, bind to potassium in the gastrointestinal tract , decreasing its absorption and increasing its elimination through the stool. However, insulin and dextrose do not directly affect gastrointestinal potassium absorption and are not the primary mechanism by which they treat hyperkalemia. Option D: Increased extracellular binding of potassium Certain medications, such as calcium gluconate , bind to potassium in the extracellular fluid, reducing its concentration and decreasing its effect on excitable tissues such as cardiac muscle. However, insulin and dextrose do not directly affect extracellular potassium binding and are not the primary mechanism by which they treat hyperkalemia. @Neet_pg_bot

An increased anion gap indicates that there is an increase in unmeasured anions , such as lactate, ketones, or sulfates, which is commonly seen in metabolic acidosis. questions.stemHtml: A 28-year-old male with a history of intravenous drug abuse is brought to the emergency department unresponsive. He is noted to have pinpoint pupils and shallow breathing. Narcan (naloxone) is administered, and the patient begins to wake up. Laboratory results show a pH of 7.0, pCO2 of 60 mmHg, and HCO3- of 24 mEq/L. What is the most likely acid-base disorder?
questions.solution: Correct Option B: Respiratory acidosis with metabolic compensation The low pH of 7.0 indicates acidosis, and the high pCO2 of 60 mmHg suggests respiratory acidosis. The normal HCO3- level of 24 mEq/L suggests metabolic compensation. The patient is experiencing opioid overdose as suggested by IV drug abuse history which leads to shallow breathing. Less CO2 is removed from the blood leading to respiratory acidosis. To maintain the pH, there is metabolic compensation in which fewer bicarbonate ions are excreted from the kidneys. Incorrect options: Option A: Metabolic acidosis with respiratory compensation It refers to an acid-base disturbance in which the primary disturbance is low bicarbonate , and the respiratory system compensates by decreasing pCO2 levels (hyperventilation). In this case, the pCO2 levels are elevated, indicating respiratory acidosis, and the HCO3- levels are normal, suggesting metabolic compensation. Option C: Metabolic alkalosis with respiratory compensation It refers to an acid-base disturbance in which the primary disturbance is elevated bicarbonate levels , and the respiratory system compensates by increasing pCO2 levels (hypoventilation). questions.solution: Correct Option A: Decreased urinary bicarbonate excretion This patient most likely suffers from acute, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) exacerbation following an upper respiratory infection. Arterial blood gas analysis showing decreased pH and increased PCO2 is consistent with respiratory acidosis. A decrease in urinary HCO3- excretion is a compensatory measure in response to hypercapnia and chronic respiratory acidosis, which often occur in patients with COPD due to expiratory airway collapse and respiratory muscle fatigue. The proximal convoluted tubules reabsorb HCO3-, improving the buffer capacity of the serum against lower pH. The kidney's distal convoluted tubules and collecting ducts increase H+ excretion (in the form of H2PO4 and NH4+), raising blood pH to compensate for respiratory acidosis. Incorrect options: Option B: Increased urinary pH This statement is incorrect, as increased urinary pH caused by the increased renal tubular excretion of HCO3- occurs as a compensatory mechanism in individuals with respiratory alkalosis. However, this patient's decreased arterial pH and increased PCO2 indicate respiratory acidosis, in which the compensatory mechanism is a decrease (not an increase) in urinary pH. Option C: Increased serum anion gap This statement is incorrect, as an increased serum anion gap occurs in high anion gap metabolic acidosis because of an accumulation of unmeasured ions (e.g., ammonium, butyrate, citrate, lactate). In respiratory acidosis, the serum anion gap typically remains unchanged. Option D: Decreased serum potassium This statement is incorrect, as hypokalemia occurs in alkalemia by shifting K+ ions from plasma into cellular compartments. Extracellular K+ exchanges with intracellular H+ as a compensatory mechanism to lower pH levels. In this patient with acidemia, hyperkalemia would be expected. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.solution: Correct Option B - Kala Azar/Leishmaniasis: The symptoms described - profound fatigue, pallor, abdominal discomfort, massive splenomegaly, anemia, jaundice, elevated levels of lactate dehydrogenase (LDH), and recurrent episodes of fever - are characteristic of visceral leishmaniasis, also known as kala-azar. It is characterized by symptoms like fever, profound fatigue, anemia, splenomegaly, hepatomegaly, and hyperpigmentation. Elevated LDH levels are also seen due to increased cell turnover. This condition is endemic in certain regions, including parts of Africa, Asia, and South America. Incorrect Options: Option A - Thalassemia Major: Thalassemia major is a genetic disorder characterized by abnormal hemoglobin production, leading to chronic anemia. While anemia is a common feature, other symptoms like fever, splenomegaly, and jaundice are not typical of thalassemia major. Option C - Mycobacterium Avium Complex: Mycobacterium avium complex (MAC) is a group of bacteria that can cause infections, particularly in individuals with weakened immune systems. It is not associated with the symptoms described in the scenario, such as anemia, splenomegaly, and jaundice. Option D - Felty Syndrome: Felty syndrome is a rare complication of rheumatoid arthritis (RA) characterized by the triad of RA, splenomegaly, and neutropenia. questions.stemHtml: A 45-year-old patient presents with fatigue, easy bruising, and recurrent infections. Physical examination reveals splenomegaly. Laboratory tests show decreased levels of red blood cells, white blood cells, and platelets. Bone marrow biopsy indicates compensatory hyperplasia. questions.solution: Correct Option C - Hypersplenism: Hypersplenism occurs when the spleen becomes overactive and removes blood cells (red blood cells, white blood cells, and platelets) from the circulation at an accelerated rate. This can lead to decreased levels of all three types of blood cells, resulting in fatigue, easy bruising, and increased susceptibility to infections. The enlarged spleen (splenomegaly) is a characteristic finding in hypersplenism. Compensatory hyperplasia of the bone marrow occurs in response to the increased demand for blood cell production. This condition fits well with the patient's clinical presentation. Incorrect Options: Option A - Hemolytic anemia: Hemolytic anemia is characterized by the destruction of red blood cells, leading to decreased levels of red blood cells and the presence of symptoms like fatigue and easy bruising. However, the presentation in the question mentions decreased levels of white blood cells and platelets as well, which is not typical of hemolytic anemia. Additionally, compensatory hyperplasia of the bone marrow is not commonly associated with hemolytic anemia. Option B – Hemophilia: Hemophilia is a genetic disorder that primarily affects blood clotting factors, leading to prolonged bleeding and easy bruising. While it can present with easy bruising and bleeding, it does not explain the decreased levels of red blood cells, white blood cells, and platelets, nor does it cause splenomegaly or bone marrow hyperplasia. Option D - Thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura (TTP): TTP is a rare disorder characterized by microvascular thrombosis, resulting in low platelet levels (thrombocytopenia) and widespread small blood vessel damage. It can lead to symptoms such as easy bruising and bleeding, but it typically presents with features like fever, neurological symptoms, and schistocytes (fragmented red blood cells) on blood smear. questions.solution: Correct Option C - IgA Deficiency: IgA Deficiency is a primary immunodeficiency disorder characterized by the absence or very low levels of immunoglobulin A (IgA) antibodies. Patients with IgA deficiency are prone to recurrent infections, particularly in mucosal surfaces like the throat and gastrointestinal tract. The finding of Peyer's patches in the intestine and the presence of specialized epithelium known as follicular associated epithelium (FAE) in the tonsils, which is a characteristic feature of mucosal immune response, is consistent with IgA deficiency. The absence of IgA compromises the mucosal immune defense, leading to increased susceptibility to infections. This diagnosis aligns with the patient's symptoms and findings. Incorrect Options: Option A - Common Variable Immunodeficiency (CVID): Common Variable Immunodeficiency (CVID) is a primary immunodeficiency disorder characterized by decreased production of antibodies, particularly immunoglobulin G (IgG) and immunoglobulin A (IgA), leading to recurrent infections. The absence of Peyer's patches in the intestine and the presence of follicular associated epithelium in the tonsils make XLA an unlikely diagnosis. Additionally, XLA is associated with absent or very small tonsils. questions.stemHtml: A 66-year-old male with a history of diabetes mellitus and hypertension presents to the emergency department complaining of sudden-onset substernal chest pain that began while he was mowing his lawn 50 minutes ago. The patient has difficulty breathing and is diaphoretic. His vital signs are stable. Physical examination shows no acute findings. An ECG reveals the results shown below. Which vessel is most likely occluded in this patient?
questions.solution: Correct Option B - First diagonal branch of LAD: This patient has a high lateral ST-elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI), presenting to the emergency department in acute distress with sudden-onset chest pain during activity. Other symptoms such as diaphoresis and shortness of breath help narrow the suspicion to myocardial infarction. The ECG shows ST elevation in leads I and aVL, which are highly specific for a high lateral myocardial infarction. Reciprocal ST depression and T-wave inversion in both main inferior leads (Leads lll and aVF) are common findings due to the direction of depolarization occurring in those leads. The most common vessels occluded in a high lateral myocardial infarction are the first diagonal branch of the left anterior descending artery or, less commonly, the obtuse marginal branch of the left circumflex artery. Incorrect Options: Option A - Left coronary artery: The left coronary artery (LCA) covers a wide range of myocardial tissue. Ischemia or infarct in LCA territory would show ST-segment changes in leads l, ll, and V4-V6. Reciprocal changes may appear in aVR. These changes are not observed in this patient’s ECG. Option C - Right coronary artery: The right coronary artery (RCA) mainly supplies the SA node and the inferior aspect of the heart. It gives off the posterior descending artery in most of the population. Occlusion of the RCA would show ST-segment changes most commonly in leads ll, lll, and aVF. Option D - Posterior descending artery: The posterior descending artery (PDA) mainly supplies the AV node, posterior third of the interventricular septum, posteromedial papillary muscle, and posterior two-thirds of the ventricular wall. Findings on this ECG do not indicate a PDA occlusion, which would usually show ST-segment depression in leads V1-V4. If posterior leads were added, ST elevation would manifest in leads V7-V9. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stemHtml: A 62-year-old male patient came to the emergency department with complaints of palpitations and sickness for the past 2 weeks. The patient has no significant history. The ECG showed bradycardia and long pauses between heartbeats. Which of the following is the diagnosis of this patient’s condition?
questions.solution: Correct Option A- Sick sinus syndrome: Sick sinus syndrome is a disorder of the sinus, which normally controls the rate and rhythm of the heart. Sick sinus syndrome presents with the symptoms of palpitations, dizziness, and fatigue. It also causes bradycardia and tachycardia. Pauses can occur in which there is no atrial or ventricular activity. Most common cause of sick sinus node syndrome is age-related wear and tear of heart tissues. With age, there is generation of the tissue, and the conduction can also be affected. On ECG, one can find bradycardia, irregular beats, or long pauses between the heartbeats. Some of the risk factors for heart disease include high blood pressure, lack of exercise, high cholesterol, etc. The ECG and Holter monitoring can diagnose this condition. This condition is treated with regular checkups. Medications are also used to treat this condition. Pacemaker and catheter ablation may be needed. Incorrect Options: Option B- Medication-induced hypotension: Certain medications can also cause palpitations and syncope due to vasodilation or decreased cardiac output. Some of the medications are diuretics, vasodilators (both arteriodilators and venodilators), beta-blockers, calcium channel blockers, etc. In old age people, an antihistamine can also cause dizziness and syncope. This can predispose patients to fall-related fractures. However, this patient's history is not significant for taking any medications. Option C- Carotid stenosis: Carotid stenosis is also common in the elderly population and can cause transient ischaemic attack and syncope due to the obstruction of the blood supply to the brain. However, this patient's ECG is consistent with the diagnosis of sick sinus syndrome, in which there can be bradycardia, long pauses between heartbeats, and irregular beats. Option D- Aortic stenosis: Aortic stenosis is common after 60 years of age. Similarly, patients with bicuspid aortic valves are predisposed to aortic stenosis. Aortic stenosis can result in decreased blood being pumped into the aorta and can result in syncope. Diuretics, vasodilators, and other drugs can also add to the effect and can result in syncope and drowsiness. This patient is not suffering from aortic stenosis. Aortic valve diameter can be seen on echocardiography. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.solution: Correct Option A - Decreased TSH: ECG demonstrates atrial fibrillation with a rapid and irregularly irregular rhythm with no discernible P-waves. The correct option is decreased TSH because this patient presents with chest pain and an ECG suggestive of atrial fibrillation. In the setting of her weight loss, protruding eyes and other symptoms of increased metabolism (such as sweating and anxiety), her atrial fibrillation is likely associated with hyperthyroidism (a decreased TSH). Atrial fibrillation typically presents with an odd sensation in the chest where the patient feels like their heart is racing. Typical causes include ischemic heart disease and connective tissue disorders ; however, hyperthyroidism is another potential cause of atrial fibrillation, and a decreased TSH level can support this diagnosis. Unstable patients should receive synchronized cardioversion. Stable patients can be given agents to slow their heart rate (such as calcium channel blockers and beta blockers). Incorrect Options: Option B - Dislodged thrombus: Pulmonary embolism is caused by dislodged thrombus which can present with chest pain, shortness of breath, and sinus tachycardia on ECG. This patient's ECG demonstrates an absence of P-waves suggesting a diagnosis of atrial fibrillation. ECG of patients with pulmonary embolism demonstrates a large S wave in lead I, a Q wave in lead III and an inverted T wave in lead III together indicate acute right heart strain. Option C - Ischemic heart disease: Ischemic heart disease presents with dull substernal chest pain and is associated with ST-elevation on ECG or a new left bundle branch block. questions.answerText: Discharge, and arrange for cardioversion within 48 hours if the patient has not spontaneously cardioverted
questions.solution: Correct Option C - Discharge, and arrange for cardioversion within 48 hours if the patient has not spontaneously cardioverted: This patient is experiencing symptomatic palpitations after consuming alcohol. His irregular heart rhythm and ECG are consistent with atrial fibrillation (AF), which has many known precipitants. These include alcohol and various prescription and illicit drugs. Given the short duration of this fibrillation episode, it is safe to convert the patient in the emergency department to sinus rhythm and arrange for cardiology follow-up. Alternatively, recent data supports that for patients who have hemodynamically stable new-onset AF for < 36 hours, it is safe to wait for up to 48 hours after symptom onset to cardiovert them (rather than early cardioversion in the emergency department) because many patients will spontaneously convert without needing electrical cardioversion or pharmacologic cardioversion. Were the AF longstanding, cardioversion might pose a risk of embolization if thrombi had formed in the ineffectively contracting atria. Either chemical or electrical cardioversion is suitable, and the first choice is usually medical cardioversion if feasible. For a first episode of AF, a patient can then be monitored for recurrence prior to considering ablation. This patient’s alcohol use must be addressed, given the potentially serious cardiac consequences. Incorrect Options: Option A - Anticoagulation for 3 months and then transesophageal echocardiogram with cardioversion: For AF of short duration, cardioversion should be performed in the emergency department upon presentation, or prior to 48 hours as an outpatient. Anticoagulation for 3 months is not necessary. Option B - Sedated unsynchronized cardioversion in the emergency department: For a stable rhythm with clear QRS complexes, it is never appropriate to perform unsynchronized cardioversion, as it may precipitate ventricular fibrillation. questions.stemHtml: A 70-year-old man came to the outpatient department for a regular follow-up. On examination, the pulse was irregular, sometimes weak and sometimes with missed beats. The patient has no underlying heart disease. ECG was done. Which of the following best describes the patient's presentation?
questions.solution: Correct Option C - Ventricular premature beats: This patient's presentation and ECG findings are consistent with ventricular premature beats. Mostly the patients are asymptomatic , but some can present with irregular or missed heartbeats or abnormally strong beats due to increased cardiac output after the ectopic beats. The ECG will show bizarre and broad complexes due to sequential activation of ventricles instead of simultaneous activation. The complexes can be: Unifocal (Identical beats arising from the same ectopic focus) Multifocal (Beats with different morphologies and arising from multiple foci) Incorrect Options: Option A - Sinus bradycardia: This patient's presentation is inconsistent with sinus bradycardia. Sinus bradycardia occurs in healthy people at rest and is commonly found in athletes. ECG includes normal sinus rhythm with a rate lower than 60 beats/min. Most patients with sinus bradycardia are asymptomatic . Symptomatic sinus bradycardia can occur in patients during MI and is treated with intravenous atropine(0.6-1.2mg). Patients with recurrent and persistently symptomatic sinus bradycardia should be managed with a pacemaker. Option B - SVT: SVT occurs in people who have no underlying structural heart disease . One episode of SVT can remain from a few seconds to hours . The patient presents with strong, forceful heart palpitations, lightheadedness, breathlessness, chest pain and discomfort . The patient can also sometimes present with polyuria due to the release of ANP . An ECG often reveals tachycardia (rate 120-240/min ) with normal QRS complexes . However, a rate-dependent bundle branch block may occasionally be present . P waves are not discernable because they are embedded in the QRS complex or small retrograde/inverted p waves seen after the QRS complex in AVNRT . This patient's presentation and ECG findings are inconsistent with SVT. Option D - Sinus tachycardia: This patient's presentation is inconsistent with sinus tachycardia as the sinus rate is not high in this patient. Patients with sinus tachycardia occur in young, healthy adults . Sinus tachycardia occurs due to increased sympathetic activity during emotional stress, exercise and pregnancy . The sinus rate can approach upto 200 beats per min during intense exercise . No treatment is needed for sinus tachycardia. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A 28-year-old woman presents to the emergency department complaining of sudden onset palpitations and chest discomfort for 30 minutes. She reports feeling anxious and lightheaded. Her vital signs are within normal limits except for a heart rate of 180/min with a regular rhythm. EKG is shown below. What is the most important finding in the EKG pointing towards supraventricular tachycardia?
questions.stemHtml: A 28-year-old woman presents to the emergency department complaining of sudden onset palpitations and chest discomfort for 30 minutes. She reports feeling anxious and lightheaded. Her vital signs are within normal limits except for a heart rate of 180/min with a regular rhythm. EKG is shown below. What is the most important finding in the EKG pointing towards supraventricular tachycardia?
questions.solution: Correct Option D - Regular narrow QRS complexes: Following are the EKG findings seen in supraventricular tachycardia. Regular narrow QRS complexes: The QRS complex width is typically < 120 ms because the electrical impulses originate in or above the atria and travel through the normal conduction system of the heart. Absent or abnormal P waves: P waves may be difficult to distinguish or absent due to the rapid rate of atrial depolarization. P-wave hidden within the QRS complex: When the electrical activity of the atria and ventricles overlap, the P wave may be hidden within the QRS complex. Inverted P waves: In some cases, the P waves may be inverted, which is seen in junctional tachycardia or AV nodal reentrant tachycardia. Shortened PR interval: The PR interval may be shortened due to the rapid conduction through the AV node. Normal or increased QT interval: The QT interval, which reflects the duration of ventricular repolarization, is typically normal or slightly prolonged in SVT. No ST-segment or T-wave abnormalities: ST-segment or T-wave changes are not typically seen in SVT. Incorrect Options: Option A - Tall T-waves: The T wave on an electrocardiogram becomes tall when there is increased electrical activity in the ventricles of the heart. It is mainly caused by hyperkalemia, ventricular hypertrophy, myocardial ischemia, and drug side effects such as digoxin. Option B - ST-elevation: ST segment is the period between the end of the QRS complex and the beginning of the T wave. It is usually elevated from normal in cases of acute myocardial infarction, pericarditis, and pulmonary embolism. Option C - Delta Waves: Delta waves appear as slurring or widening of the QRS complex on an ECG. Specifically, delta waves are seen in patients with Wolff-Parkinson-White (WPW) syndrome , a condition in which there is an additional electrical pathway in the heart. @Neet_pg_bot
