Physical exam reveals jugular venous distension, bibasilar crackles, and an S3 gallop. His serum BNP level is elevated. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.stemHtml: A 65-year-old male with a history of hypertension presents to the emergency department with dyspnea, orthopnea, and bilateral lower extremity oedema. Physical exam reveals jugular venous distension, bibasilar crackles, and an S3 gallop. His serum BNP level is elevated. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.solution: Correct Option D- Heart failure: The clinical presentation of dyspnea, orthopnea, bilateral lower extremity oedema, jugular venous distension, bibasilar crackles, and an S3 gallop, in addition to an elevated serum BNP level, are highly suggestive of heart failure. Heart failure is a common clinical syndrome that occurs as a result of the heart's inability to pump enough blood to meet the body's metabolic demands. It can be caused by several factors, including hypertension, coronary artery disease, valvular disease, and cardiomyopathy. Incorrect Options: Option A- Acute myocardial infarction: Acute myocardial infarction (AMI) can cause heart failure, but it typically presents with chest pain, electrocardiographic changes, and elevated cardiac biomarkers, such as troponin. In this case, the patient did not present with chest pain, and his troponin level was not mentioned, making AMI an unlikely diagnosis. Option B- Aortic stenosis: Aortic stenosis is a condition where the aortic valve narrows, leading to reduced blood flow from the left ventricle to the aorta. Patients with aortic stenosis may present with chest pain, syncope, and dyspnea on exertion. However, in this case, the patient’s presented with orthopnea and bilateral lower extremity oedema, which are not typical symptoms of aortic stenosis, making it an unlikely diagnosis. Option C- Pulmonary embolism: Pulmonary embolism (PE) is a life-threatening condition that occurs when a blood clot travels to the lungs, obstructing blood flow. questions.stem: A 14-year-old boy is in the middle of a basketball game when he suddenly becomes dizzy and collapses. An ambulance is called. He has no prior medical problems and was thought to have a benign murmur on his previous physical examination. When paramedics arrive, the patient is awake but uncomfortable, and complaining of a rapid heart rate. While the ECG (shown below) is obtained, he loses consciousness and becomes pulseless. With initiation of CPR and the application of a defibrillator, he regains a normal rhythm. During his ensuing workup, which test will likely diagnose the cause of this episode?
questions.stemHtml: A 14-year-old boy is in the middle of a basketball game when he suddenly becomes dizzy and collapses. An ambulance is called. He has no prior medical problems and was thought to have a benign murmur on his previous physical examination. When paramedics arrive, the patient is awake but uncomfortable, and complaining of a rapid heart rate. While the ECG (shown below) is obtained, he loses consciousness and becomes pulseless. With initiation of CPR and the application of a defibrillator, he regains a normal rhythm. During his ensuing workup, which test will likely diagnose the cause of this episode?
questions.solution: Correct Option B - An echocardiogram: This patient has a history of a murmur and lost consciousness during physical exertion. The cause must be considered to be cardiac until proven otherwise. The ECG shown demonstrates ventricular tachycardia degenerating into ventricular fibrillation, which is rapidly fatal unless advanced life support is initiated. The most frequent causes of ventricular fibrillation in this age group are inherited arrhythmias an d hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy , which can cause abnormal rhythms during exercise and is the most likely possibility in this case. The diagnosis can be made definitively by echocardiography , with more advanced imaging used to determine risk. Incorrect Options: Option A - An exercise stress test: Conducting a stress test would not be advised in a patient who had experienced a life-threatening arrhythmia during exercise. Option C - A nuclear myocardial perfusion scan : This test is also primarily used to assess blood flow to the heart muscle and is typically indicated for evaluating coronary artery disease. It may not be the most appropriate test for a young patient who experienced a sudden cardiac event. Option D - A Holter monitor: A myocardial perfusion scan demonstrate ischemia and local cardiac metabolism, not cardiac anatomy. A teenager is unlikely to have ischemic heart disease. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A 30-year-old woman comes to the physician due to a one-month history of weight gain and facial oedema. Her blood pressure is 140/80 mm Hg, her pulse is 80/min, and her examination shows 2+ ankle oedema. Urine analysis shows 3+ proteinuria and fatty casts. Which of the following is most likely the cause of her proteinuria?
questions.stemHtml: A 30-year-old woman comes to the physician due to a one-month history of weight gain and facial oedema. Her blood pressure is 140/80 mm Hg, her pulse is 80/min, and her examination shows 2+ ankle oedema. Urine analysis shows 3+ proteinuria and fatty casts. Which of the following is most likely the cause of her proteinuria?
questions.solution: Correct Option B: Glomerular proteinuria The patient, in this case, has nephrotic syndrome. Nephrotic syndrome is a clinical syndrome characterized by the following: Proteinuria (> 3-3.5 g/day - most important manifestation) Hypoalbuminemia Edema Hyperlipidemia and lipiduria The basic pathology is the altered permeability of the glomerular membrane for proteins. Diseases most commonly causing nephrotic syndrome are: Minimal change disease (in children) Membranous glomerulopathy (adults) Mesangial proliferative glomerulonephritis Membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis Focal segmental glomerulosclerosis Proteinuria is excessive protein excretion in the urine, generally greater than 150 mg daily in adults. Proteinuria can be associated with high serum creatinine levels, elevated blood urea nitrogen (BUN) or evidence of systemic illness (e.g., fever, rash, vasculitis). Glomerular proteinuria is a medical condition characterized by excess protein in the urine due to abnormalities in the glomerular filtration barrier in the kidneys. The glomerular filtration barrier is a complex structure comprising three layers: the fenestrated endothelium, the basement membrane, and the podocytes. This barrier is responsible for filtering out waste products and excess fluid from the blood while preventing larger molecules, such as proteins, from entering the urine. Glomerular proteinuria can occur when there is damage or disruption to any of these layers, which can lead to the passage of protein into the urine. It results from the effacement of epithelial cell foot processes and altered glomerular permeability with an increased filtration fraction of normal plasma proteins, as in diabetic nephropathy. Protein electrophoresis will have a pattern exhibiting a large albumin spike indicative of the increased permeability of albumin across the damaged GBM. Incorrect options: Option A: Functional proteinuria Functional proteinuria is not due to any underlying disease or medical condition but a functional body response to certain stressors. This type of proteinuria is usually benign and self-limiting and does not require any specific treatment. Functional proteinuria can be caused by a variety of factors, including: Exercise Fever Emotional stress Dehydration Functional proteinuria is a benign process resulting from acute illness, exercise, and "orthostatic proteinuria." Orthostatic proteinuria usually causes protein excretion of less than 1 g/day. It occurs only during the daytime and is associated with an upright posture. This patient has a history of nephrotic syndrome, so functional proteinuria is unlikely. Option C: Tubular proteinuria Tubular proteinuria is a medical condition characterized by excess protein in the urine due to abnormalities in the reabsorption of proteins by the tubular cells in the kidneys. Normally, the kidney tubular cells reabsorb small amounts of protein that pass through the glomeruli and into the filtrate. However, in tubular proteinuria, there is a defect in the tubular cells that impairs their ability to reabsorb proteins, leading to increased protein levels in the urine. It occurs as the reabsorption of normally filtered proteins in the proximal tubule is defective. It occurs due to a variety of causes: Acute tubular necrosis Toxic injury (lead, aminoglycosides and certain antiretrovirals), Drug-induced interstitial nephritis Hereditary metabolic disorders (Wilson disease and Fanconi syndrome). Option D: Overload proteinuria Overload proteinuria is a medical condition characterized by excess protein in the urine due to abnormal blood proteins that exceed the renal tubules' reabsorptive capacity. In this type of proteinuria, the excess protein is not due to a defect in the glomerular filtration barrier or tubular reabsorption but rather due to an excess of abnormal proteins that the renal tubules cannot properly reabsorb. Overload proteinuria can result from: Overproduction of circulating, filterable plasma proteins (monoclonal gammopathies), such as Bence Jones proteins associated with plasma cell myeloma (formerly multiple myeloma). Amyloidosis: Amyloidosis is a condition in which abnormal proteins build up in various tissues in the body, including the kidneys, and can lead to overflow proteinuria. Sickle cell disease: Sickle cell disease can cause the breakdown of red blood cells, releasing hemoglobin into the blood and urine, leading to overflow proteinuria. Fabry disease: It is a genetic disorder in which a buildup of a specific type of fat in the body can produce abnormal proteins that can be excreted in the urine, leading to overflow proteinuria. Protein electrophoresis from the serum or urine will exhibit a discrete protein peak. Other examples of overload proteinuria include myoglobinuria in rhabdomyolysis and hemoglobinuria in hemolysis. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A 40-year-old man presents to the emergency department with shortness of breath and confusion. Arterial blood gas (ABG) analysis reveals respiratory acidosis. Which of the following structures in the kidney is responsible for regulating acid-base balance?
questions.stemHtml: A 40-year-old man presents to the emergency department with shortness of breath and confusion. Arterial blood gas (ABG) analysis reveals respiratory acidosis. Which of the following structures in the kidney is responsible for regulating acid-base balance?
questions.solution: Option C- Proximal tubule: The kidneys play a key role in regulating the acid-base balance of the body by removing excess acid or base from the blood. The proximal tubule is the primary site of acid-base regulation in the kidney, where bicarbonate ions (HCO3-) are reabsorbed from the filtrate and returned to the bloodstream. Bicarbonate ions are important for buffering acids in the blood and maintaining a pH that is compatible with normal bodily functions. When there is an excess of acid in the blood, such as in the case of respiratory acidosis, the kidneys respond by increasing the reabsorption of bicarbonate ions in the proximal tubule, which helps to neutralise the excess acid and restore the acid-base balance of the body. This process is regulated by several mechanisms, including the action of carbonic anhydrase enzymes in the proximal tubule, which catalyse the conversion of carbon dioxide (CO2) and water (H2O) into carbonic acid (H2CO3), which dissociates into bicarbonate ions and hydrogen ions (H+). The hydrogen ions are secreted into the filtrate in exchange for the reabsorption of bicarbonate ions, which are then returned to the bloodstream to help buffer excess acid. Therefore, option C is correct because the proximal tubule is responsible for regulating acid-base balance in the kidney. Incorrect Options: Option A- Glomerulus: The glomerulus is responsible for filtering blood and removing waste products from the bloodstream, but it is not directly involved in regulating acid-base balance in the kidney. The glomerulus is a network of capillaries in the renal corpuscle that is responsible for filtering blood and producing a filtrate that contains water, electrolytes, and waste products. The filtrate produced by the glomerulus is then modified as it passes through the renal tubules, where various substances are reabsorbed back into the bloodstream or secreted into the urine. While the glomerulus is not directly involved in acid-base regulation, it does play a role in maintaining the electrolyte balance of the body by filtering out excess sodium and other electrolytes from the blood. Therefore, option A is incorrect because the glomerulus is not responsible for regulating acid-base balance in the kidney. Option B- Bowman's capsule: Bowman's capsule is the cup-shaped structure that surrounds the glomerulus in the renal corpuscle and collects the filtrate that is produced by the glomerulus. While Bowman's capsule is involved in the initial filtration of blood in the kidney, it is not directly involved in the regulation of acid-base balance. Once the filtrate is collected in Bowman's capsule, it then passes into the renal tubules where it is modified and processed. Therefore, option B is incorrect because Bowman's capsule is not responsible for regulating acid-base balance in the kidney. Option D- Distal tubule: The distal tubule is a part of the renal tubule that comes after the loop of Henle and is responsible for fine-tuning the concentration of urine by reabsorbing some ions and water and secreting others. While the distal tubule plays a role in regulating the balance of electrolytes in the body, it is not primarily responsible for regulating acid-base balance in the kidney. The distal tubule does have some capacity to regulate acid-base balance, but its primary function is the regulation of salt and water balance in the body. Therefore, option D is incorrect because the distal tubule is not primarily responsible for regulating acid-base balance in the kidney. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A 65-year-old man with a 3-month history of shortness of breath on exertion. He mentions that he cannot lie down for long and has to get up to catch his breath. This is affecting his sleep as well. He feels difficulty when tries to walk long distances. On auscultation of the chest, the lung sounds are reduced and the apical pulse is displaced. An additional heart sound after S2 is heard as well. The patient’s chest X-ray reveals an enlarged cardiac shadow with bilateral pulmonary edema. What could be the most likely electrolyte imbalance in this case?
questions.stemHtml: A 65-year-old man with a 3-month history of shortness of breath on exertion. He mentions that he cannot lie down for long and has to get up to catch his breath. This is affecting his sleep as well. He feels difficulty when tries to walk long distances. On auscultation of the chest, the lung sounds are reduced and the apical pulse is displaced. An additional heart sound after S2 is heard as well. The patient’s chest X-ray reveals an enlarged cardiac shadow with bilateral pulmonary edema. What could be the most likely electrolyte imbalance in this case?
questions.solution: Correct Option B-Hyponatremia: This patient is experiencing Congestive Heart Failure as suggested by enlarged cardiac shadow on chest X-ray, displaced apical pulse and additional heart sound (most likely S3) on auscultation of the chest. Congestive heart failure can lead to hyponatremia due to the release of antidiuretic hormone (ADH) from the pituitary gland in response to decreased cardiac output. This leads to water retention and dilutional hyponatremia. The normal range for serum sodium concentration is 135-145 mEq/ L. Symptoms of hyponatremia can include generalized weakness, fatigue, and confusion. Incorrect Options: Option A- Hypernatremia: Hypernatremia refers to high serum sodium levels i.e. above 145 mEq/L . It is typically caused by dehydration or excessive sodium intake. This patient's findings are suggestive of congestive heart failure which makes this option less likely. Option C- Hyperkalemia: Hyperkalemia refers to high serum potassium levels ( normal range = 3.2-5.7 mEq/L). It can be caused by some factors such as renal failure, medication use, or metabolic acidosis. However, this option is less likely given the patient's symptoms which are suggestive of Congestive Cardiac Failure. Option D- Hypocalcemia: Hypocalcemia refers to low serum calcium levels ( normal range 4.4-5.2 mEq/L). It can be caused by low calcium intake, disorders of vitamin D synthesis, hypoparathyroidism or chronic renal failure. Classical signs are peri-oral or peripheral paresthesias, abdominal pain, Chevostek Sign (twitching of facial muscles after tapping the facial nerve) and Trousseau Sign (carpal spasm when the brachial artery is occluded with a BP cuff). In this case, hypocalcemia is least likely. @Neet_pg_bot

  • The normal range for serum sodium concentration is 135-145 mEq/L.
  • Symptoms of hyponatremia can include generalized weakness, fatigue, and confusion.

Incorrect Options:

Option A- Hypernatremia:

  • Hypernatremia refers to high serum sodium levels i.e. above 145 mEq/L.

Option C- Hyperkalemia:

  • Hyperkalemia refers to high serum potassium levels (normal range = 3.2-5.7 mEq/L).

  • Hypocalcemia refers to low serum calcium levels ( normal range 4.4-5.2 mEq/L).

questions.stemHtml: A 45-year-old male presents to a clinic with complaints of lethargy, dizziness, nausea, vomiting and abdominal pain for one day. He has a history of hypertension and systemic lupus erythematosus. He is on prednisolone and nifedipine for five years. Examination reveals a soft and non-tender abdomen with central obesity. The investigation of the patient reveals a decreased concentration of serum ACTH and cortisol. Which of the following findings can also be seen in this patient?
questions.solution: Correct Option C: Hyponatremia This is a case of tertiary adrenal insufficiency in which the patient presents with complaints of lethargy, dizziness, nausea, vomiting and abdominal pain for one day. The patient in this case also has a history of hypertension and systemic lupus erythematosus for which he is using prednisolone and nifedipine . The chronic use of prednisolone increases the risk of adrenal insufficiency. An examination of the patient was done which revealed a soft and non-tender abdomen along with central obesity . An investigation of the patient was done which revealed a decrease in the concentration of serum ACTH and cortisol . All these signs and symptoms along with the investigational findings suggest tertiary adrenal insufficiency . The tertiary adrenal insufficiency caused by to use of corticosteroids is usually associated with hyponatremia. It is caused because of increased antidiuretic hormone secretion (ADH). ADH secretion is usually inhibited by cortisol . In this case, there is decreased cortisol which results in an increase in ADH. Incorrect options: Option A: Hyperkalemia Hyperkalemia usually occurs in those cases in which there is a decrease in the secretion of aldosterone . It is usually seen in primary adrenal insufficiency . In this case, aldosterone secretion is preserved. So, there will be a normal level of potassium in this case. Option B: Hyperglycemia Hyperglycemia is one of the most common side effects in those patients who are using glucocorticoids. However, in this case, glucogenesis is not stimulated by cortisol because of its decreased level. Thus, the patient in this case can have hypoglycemia instead of hyperglycemia. Option D: Hypokalemia Hypokalemia can result when there is excessive renal loss which can be due to many conditions includ ing Cushing syndrome, hyperaldosteronism and renal tubular acidosis . The potassium level is usually normal in cases of adrenal insufficiency because aldosterone secretion is preserved. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.solution: Correct Option C- Monitoring signs of cerebral edema: In a patient with hypernatremia, sodium concentration is more than 145mEq/L and serum osmolality is greater which causes fluid to shift from the intracellular compartment and cause the cells to shrink Cells adapt to this change in chronic hypernatremia as in the case of elderly patients in which long-standing decreased oral fluid intake cause this hypernatremia When the patient with hypernatremia is treated then these chronic patients should be managed carefully as the rapid correction of hypernatremia in these patient decreases serum osmolality and cause fluid to shift intracellularly and cells swell up This is most important in the brain as it causes cerebral edema and signs and symptoms of neurologic dysfunction Serum sodium should not be decreased by more than 12mEq/L in 24 hours period and 0.5mEq/L per hour So close monitoring of the patient for every 2 to 4 hours for serum sodium and checking for the signs questions.solutionHtml:
Correct Option C- Monitoring signs of cerebral edema:

  • In a patient with hypernatremia, sodium concentration is more than 145mEq/L and serum osmolality is greater which causes fluid to shift from the intracellular compartment and cause the cells to shrink
  • Cells adapt to this change in chronic hypernatremia as in the case of elderly patients in which long-standing decreased oral fluid intake cause this hypernatremia
  • When the patient with hypernatremia is treated then these chronic patients should be managed carefully as the rapid correction of hypernatremia in these patient decreases serum osmolality and cause fluid to shift intracellularly and cells swell up
  • This is most important in the brain as it causes cerebral edema and signs and symptoms of neurologic dysfunction
  • Serum sodium should not be decreased by more than 12mEq/L in 24 hours period and 0.5mEq/L per hour
  • So close monitoring of the patient for every 2 to 4 hours for serum sodium and checking for the signs and symptoms of cerebral edema like seizures or any neurologic dysfunction is important

Incorrect Options:

Option A- Monitoring blood glucose level:

  • Monitoring blood glucose levels is important in diabetic patients if they present with high blood glucose levels and positive serum ketones to manage the diabetic ketoacidosis
  • If the blood glucose level is mildly elevated and ketones are negative then blood glucose level monitoring is less important than the management of hypernatremia and its complications in these patients

Option B- Monitoring serum ketones level:

  • Serum ketones are monitored in patients when the presentation is of diabetic ketoacidosis like the fruity smell of the breath, acidic pH, positive serum ketones, and high blood glucose level level
  • If the blood glucose level is normal and ketones are negative then serum ketones monitoring is unnecessary

Option D- Monitoring for urine output:

  • Urine output monitoring is important in severe hypovolemia, decreased blood pressure, and oliguria
  • If the blood pressure and urine output are slightly decreased then monitoring is of secondary importance as compared to monitoring for signs of cerebral edema

questions.stemHtml: A 63-year-old man presents with decreased urination for the last day. He has a history of diabetes mellitus and hypertension for the last 20 years and is non-compliant with his medications. On examination, his blood pressure is 170/90 mmHg, his random blood sugar level is 303 mg/dL, and his creatinine and urea levels are 3.4 mg/dL and 63 mg/dL, respectively. His serum calcium levels are 11.01 mg/dL. Which of the following parts of the nephron reabsorbs the most calcium?
questions.solution: Correct Option A- Proximal convoluted tubules: The human kidneys play a vital role in regulating calcium balance in the body. Any abnormality in the functionality of the kidneys may also affect the renal excretion of calcium. Around 100mg to 200mg of calcium is excreted normally per day during urination, and of the filtered load, about 98% of calcium is reabsorbed within the nephrons. The proximal convoluted tubule is involved in reabsorbing the major bulk of calcium, making around 60% to 70%. Calcium reabsorption in the proximal convoluted tubule occurs by passive diffusion and solvent drag. The loop of Henle is responsible for 20% of calcium reabsorption. In comparison, the distal convoluted tubule and collecting duct reabsorb around 10% and 5% of the calcium, respectively. There are various fractions of serum calcium: ionised or free calcium (approximately 40%), bound to protein (approximately 45%), and complexed to phosphate and citrate (approximately 15%). Incorrect Options: Option B- Loop of Henle: The loop of Henle is responsible for 20% of calcium reabsorption within the nephron. In comparison, the proximal convoluted tubule is involved in reabsorbing the major bulk of calcium, making around 60% to 70%. Option C- Distal convoluted tubule: The distal convoluted tubule also takes part in reabsorbing the calcium. It reabsorbs about 10% of the filtered calcium. In comparison, the proximal convoluted tubule is involved in reabsorbing the major bulk of calcium, making around 60% to 70%. Option D- Collecting duct: The collecting duct of the nephron accounts for reabsorbing around 5% of the filtered calcium. In comparison, the proximal convoluted tubule is involved in reabsorbing the major bulk of calcium, making around 60% to 70%. @Neet_pg_bot

He also reports increased urination and thirst but denies any recent illness or injury. He has a past medical history of recurrent kidney stones and is currently taking potassium citrate for prevention. Physical examination is significant for hypotension. Laboratory investigations show hypokalemia, metabolic alkalosis, and hyperreninemic hyperaldosteronism. Urine analysis shows low urinary chloride levels and high potassium, magnesium, and calcium levels. Ultrasound of the kidneys reveals nephrocalcinosis. Genetic testing is performed, and the patient is diagnosed with Bartter Syndrome. What is the most likely pathophysiology involved in this syndrome?

Laboratory investigations show hypokalemia, metabolic alkalosis, and hyperreninemic hyperaldosteronism. Urine analysis shows low urinary chloride levels and high potassium, magnesium, and calcium levels. Ultrasound of the kidneys reveals nephrocalcinosis. Genetic testing is performed, and the patient is diagnosed with Bartter Syndrome. What is the most likely pathophysiology involved in this syndrome?

options.label: A

options.label: B

questions.answerText: Defective reabsorption of sodium and chloride in the thick ascending loop of Henle.
questions.solution: Correct Option C- Defective reabsorption of sodium and chloride in the thick ascending loop of henle: Bartter Syndrome is characterized by a defect in salt reabsorption in the thick ascending limb of the loop of Henle, leading to excessive urinary losses of sodium and chloride in the distal tubule. This defect is due to mutations in genes encoding for ion channels and transporters that regulate salt reabsorption in the loop of Henle. Defective reabsorption of sodium and chloride in the distal tubule leads to hypokalemia, metabolic alkalosis, and hyperreninemic hyperaldosteronism. Clinical Features: Muscle weakness, fatigue, and cramps Polyuria, polydipsia, and dehydration Growth failure, developmental delay, and intellectual disability (in severe cases) Nephrolithiasis, nephrocalcinosis, and renal failure (in some cases) Lab Investigations: Hypokalemia, metabolic alkalosis, and hyperreninemic hyperaldosteronism Low urinary chloride levels (less than 20 mEq/L) High urinary potassium, magnesium, and calcium levels Imaging Findings: Ultrasonography may reveal nephrocalcinosis, which is the deposition of calcium in the renal parenchyma. Treatment Options for Bartter Syndrome: Potassium and magnesium supplementation to correct electrolyte imbalances. Reduce renal prostaglandin production with non-steroidal anti-inflammatory medications. Incorrect Options: Option A- Sodium reabsorption in the ascending loop of Henle is increased: It describes a different condition called Hypotonic Hyponatremia Syndrome, also known as reset osmostat or hypotonic dehydration syndrome. In this condition, there is a resetting of the osmostat in the hypothalamus, leading to a lower-than-normal set point for plasma osmolality. It leads to increased sodium reabsorption in the descending limb of the loop of Henle, resulting in hypotonic hyponatremia and decreased urine output. Lab Investigations: Low serum sodium levels (< 135 mEq/L) Low plasma osmolality (< 280 mOsm/kg) Low urinary sodium and chloride levels MRI may reveal hypothalamic abnormalities or tumors. Option B- Decreased secretion of aldosterone in the adrenal cortex: It describes a different condition called Hypoaldosteronism Syndrome. There is decreased aldosterone secretion from the adrenal cortex, leading to electrolyte imbalances and renal dysfunction. Aldosterone plays a crucial role in regulating sodium and potassium balance in the body and a decrease in aldosterone levels can lead to hyponatremia (low sodium levels in the blood), hyperkalemia (high potassium levels in the blood), and metabolic acidosis. Lab Investigations: Low serum aldosterone levels Low sodium and high potassium levels in the blood Metabolic acidosis Imaging Findings: MRI may reveal adrenal gland abnormalities or damage. Option D- Decreased secretion of antidiuretic hormone (ADH) from the pituitary gland: It describes a different condition called Diabetes Insipidus. It occurs by a deficiency in ADH secretion or action can result from damage to the pituitary gland or hypothalamus, a genetic defect, or medications. ADH plays a crucial role in regulating water balance in the body, and a decrease in ADH levels can lead to excessive urine output and dehydration. Clinical Features: Polyuria and polydipsia Lab Investigations: Low serum ADH levels Increased serum sodium levels and decreased urine specific gravity Water deprivation test to distinguish between central and nephrogenic diabetes insipidus. Imaging Findings for Diabetes Insipidus: MRI may reveal pituitary gland abnormalities or damage. @Neet_pg_bot

Correct Option C- Defective reabsorption of sodium and chloride in the thick ascending loop of henle:

  • Bartter Syndrome is characterized by a defect in salt reabsorption in the thick ascending limb of the loop of Henle, leading to excessive urinary losses of sodium and chloride in the distal tubule.
  • This defect is due to mutations in genes encoding for ion channels and transporters that regulate salt reabsorption in the loop of Henle.
  • Defective reabsorption of sodium and chloride in the distal tubule leads to hypokalemia, metabolic alkalosis, and hyperreninemic hyperaldosteronism.
  • Clinical Features:
    • Muscle weakness, fatigue, and cramps
    • Polyuria, polydipsia, and dehydration
    • Growth failure, developmental delay, and intellectual disability (in severe cases)
    • Nephrolithiasis, nephrocalcinosis, and renal failure (in some cases)
  • Lab Investigations:
    • Hypokalemia, metabolic alkalosis, and hyperreninemic hyperaldosteronism
    • Low urinary chloride levels (less than 20 mEq/L)
    • High urinary potassium, magnesium, and calcium levels
  • Imaging Findings:
    • Ultrasonography may reveal nephrocalcinosis, which is the deposition of calcium in the renal parenchyma.
  • Treatment Options for Bartter Syndrome:
    • Potassium and magnesium supplementation to correct electrolyte imbalances.
    • Reduce renal prostaglandin production with non-steroidal anti-inflammatory medications.

Incorrect Options:

Option A- Sodium reabsorption in the ascending loop of Henle is increased:

  • It describes a different condition called Hypotonic Hyponatremia Syndrome, also known as reset osmostat or hypotonic dehydration syndrome.
  • In this condition, there is a resetting of the osmostat in the hypothalamus, leading to a lower-than-normal set point for plasma osmolality.
  • It leads to increased sodium reabsorption in the descending limb of the loop of Henle, resulting in hypotonic hyponatremia and decreased urine output.
  • Lab Investigations:
    • Low serum sodium levels (< 135 mEq/L)
    • Low plasma osmolality (< 280 mOsm/kg)
    • Low urinary sodium and chloride levels
  • MRI may reveal hypothalamic abnormalities or tumors.

Option B- Decreased secretion of aldosterone in the adrenal cortex:

  • It describes a different condition called Hypoaldosteronism Syndrome.
  • There is decreased aldosterone secretion from the adrenal cortex, leading to electrolyte imbalances and renal dysfunction.
  • Aldosterone plays a crucial role in regulating sodium and potassium balance in the body and a decrease in aldosterone levels can lead to hyponatremia (low sodium levels in the blood), hyperkalemia (high potassium levels in the blood), and metabolic acidosis.
  • Lab Investigations:
    • Low serum aldosterone levels
    • Low sodium and high potassium levels in the blood
    • Metabolic acidosis
  • Imaging Findings:
    • MRI may reveal adrenal gland abnormalities or damage.

Option D- Decreased secretion of antidiuretic hormone (ADH) from the pituitary gland:

  • It describes a different condition called Diabetes Insipidus.
  • It occurs by a deficiency in ADH secretion or action can result from damage to the pituitary gland or hypothalamus, a genetic defect, or medications.
  • ADH plays a crucial role in regulating water balance in the body, and a decrease in ADH levels can lead to excessive urine output and dehydration.
  • Clinical Features:
    • Polyuria and polydipsia
  • Lab Investigations:
    • Low serum ADH levels
    • Increased serum sodium levels and decreased urine specific gravity
    • Water deprivation test to distinguish between central and nephrogenic diabetes insipidus.
  • Imaging Findings for Diabetes Insipidus:
    • MRI may reveal pituitary gland abnormalities or damage.

questions.solution: Correct Option B- Continue with hemodialysis with modification: Hemodialysis involves using an artificial kidney machine to filter blood through a dialyzer . Which of the following is the most appropriate indication for renal transplantation in this patient?
questions.stemHtml: A 45-year-old man with end-stage renal disease due to polycystic kidney disease has presented to the physician's clinic. He has been on hemodialysis for the past six months and has a history of hypertension and diabetes mellitus type 2. Which of the following is the most appropriate indication for renal transplantation in this patient?
questions.solution: Correct Option C- Symptomatic uremia: Patients with end-stage renal disease (Irreversible kidney dysfunction with eGFR < 15 mL/min/1.73 m2) often experience a range of symptoms due to the accumulation of waste products and the loss of kidney function. These symptoms, collectively known as uremia, can include fatigue, nausea, vomiting, pericarditis, peripheral neuropathy pleuritis, lethargy, confusion, seizures, somnolence, coma, and pruritus. There is increased bleeding risk and infection. Renal transplantation is a well-established treatment for uremia , as it can restore kidney function and alleviate these symptoms. Incorrect Options: Option A- Uncontrolled hypertension: Although hypertension is a common complication of end-stage renal disease, it does not indicate renal transplantation. Hypertension can usually be managed with medications and lifestyle changes, and kidney transplantation may not necessarily improve hypertension control. Option B- Poor glycemic control: While diabetes mellitus is a common cause of end-stage renal disease, poor glycemic control does not indicate renal transplantation. Transplantation may improve glucose control in some patients, but other treatments can also achieve glycemic control . Option D- Polycystic kidney disease: Polycystic kidney disease (PKD) is a genetic disorder that causes cysts to form in the kidneys, leading to progressive kidney damage and end-stage renal disease. PKD is a common indication for renal transplantation, as it is usually irreversible and can only be treated by replacing the damaged kidneys with a healthy donor kidney. @Neet_pg_bot

Which test will provide the greatest sensitivity on a specimen collected from the anal sores?

questions.solution: Correct Option A - Rapid, multiplex, real-time PCR Lymphogranuloma venereum (LGV) is caused by Chlamydia trachomatis serovars L1, L2 and L3, which are distinct from those that cause the more common form of Chlamydial disease (serovars D-K). The LGV strains are most often found in Africa, Southeastern Asia, Latin America, and the Caribbean. Sporadic cases of LGV have occurred in North America, although these are thought to have been imported. During the first phase of the infection, patients present with an ulcerative disease. These ulcers are usually small and of short duration. After the resolution of the ulcers, there are two main presentations of this disease: the classical inguinal syndrome as well as the anorectal syndrome. In the inguinal syndrome, the bacteria spread via the lymphatic system to cause inguinal lymphadenopathy with the formation of buboes. If the disease is left untreated, the surrounding tissue structures can be destroyed, leading to fistulas and damage to the lymphatic system. In severe cases, it may result in elephantiasis. Typical anorectal symptoms include spasms, perianal sores, bloody discharge, pain, and constipation (as in this case). Multiplex real-time PCR is specific for the detection of LGV associated L-serovars and enables the differentiation of L1, L2, and L3 for epidemiologic studies. Option C - Serology with complement fixation: Serology with complement fixation can support the diagnosis of LGV (complement fixation titers >1:64), but these methods are not standardized. Hence, there is limited information about how well they perform or how to interpret the results. Option D - Genetic probe method: Genetic probe methods may be accurate but are not as sensitive as nucleic acid amplification methods. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stemHtml: A 75-year-old patient is admitted to the hospital for respiratory distress and is treated for influenza. After 5 days of treatment, he continues to have a fever. On day 8, the nurse inquires about removing droplet precautions. What is the most appropriate course of action?

options.label: B

questions.answerText: Continue droplet precautions until the fever is resolved
questions.solution: Correct Option A - Continue droplet precautions until the fever is resolved Influenza is predominantly transmitted via droplets. The virus is shed from the airway and spread by coughing and sneezing. Other ways of transmission are of lesser importance. Shedding of the virus may continue despite treatment. The current recommendation indicates that droplet precautions can be dropped after 7 days from the onset of the illness or 24 hours after resolution of the symptoms (whichever is longer). In this particular example, the patient experienced a fever, so isolation precaution should be continued. Incorrect Options: Option B - Discontinue droplet precautions since the patient finished treatment: This option is incorrect because the patient still has a fever after 5 days of influenza treatment. Even though the patient completed the treatment course, the persistence of the fever suggests that the infection may not have completely resolved. Droplet precautions should be continued until the fever has resolved to prevent the potential spread of the infection to others. Option C - Relocate the patient to a negative-pressure room: This option is also incorrect. Negative-pressure rooms are typically used for patients with airborne infections, such as tuberculosis or measles, where the infectious particles can remain suspended in the air for an extended period. Influenza is primarily transmitted through respiratory droplets, not through the airborne route. Thus, relocating the patient to a negative-pressure room is not necessary in this case. Option D - Repeat treatment with Tamiflu: This option is incorrect because it assumes that the patient's fever is persisting due to an inadequate response to the initial Tamiflu treatment. However, it's important to note that some patients with influenza, especially elderly individuals or those with compromised immune systems, may experience a prolonged fever even after appropriate antiviral treatment. Repeating Tamiflu without any clinical indication may not be necessary and could lead to potential side effects without any significant benefit. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.solution: Correct Option B- Trophozoite stage: The trophozoite stage of the malarial parasites is responsible for the clinical symptoms of malaria. During this stage, the parasites actively invade and multiply within red blood cells, leading to the characteristic fever, chills, and other systemic manifestations. Incorrect Options: Option A- Sporozoite stage: Sporozoites are the infectious form transmitted to humans by Anopheles mosquitoes. They travel to the liver and undergo maturation, but they do not directly cause clinical symptoms. Option C-Schizont stage: Schizonts are the stage where the parasites mature and divide within the liver cells before releasing merozoites into the bloodstream. While a burst of schizonts can lead to the release of merozoites and subsequent clinical symptoms, it is the trophozoite stage that predominantly causes symptoms within red blood cells. Option D- Gametocytes stage: Gametocytes are the sexual forms of the parasite that are taken up by mosquitoes during a blood meal, contributing to the transmission of malaria. They do not directly cause clinical symptoms in the human host. @Neet_pg_bot

She has a history of systemic lupus erythematosus, for which she is receiving treatment. On examination, she had a pulse of 88 bpm regular, blood pressure of 122/80 mmHg, and a temperature of 37oC. Cardiovascular examination revealed normal heart sounds and chest examination was normal. Investigations revealed normal FBC, U+Es, and LFTs. Her six-hour troponin concentration was 12 (<14). ECG revealed sinus rhythm with ST elevation in the lateral leads. CXR was normal. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.stemHtml:

Investigations revealed normal FBC, U+Es, and LFTs. Her six-hour troponin concentration was 12 (&lt;14). ECG revealed sinus rhythm with ST elevation in the lateral leads. CXR was normal.

questions.solution: Correct Option A - Autoimmune pericarditis: The history is highly suggestive of pericarditis with the exacerbation of the pain on lying flat. A six-hour troponin that is below 14 strongly argues against a diagnosis of acute coronary syndrome. In the context of SLE, the diagnosis is most likely an auto-immune pericarditis. Pericarditis in SLE occurs in roughly 25% of patients, though many may be subclinical. Incorrect Options: Option B - Autoimmune pleuritis: In the given scenario, the patient's pain is described as worse lying flat, and there is ST elevation on the ECG, which are not typical features of pleuritis. The ST elevation suggests myocardial involvement, making autoimmune pleuritis less likely. Additionally, the acute nature of the symptoms and the patient's underlying condition point more toward autoimmune pericarditis as a diagnosis. Option D - Libman–Sacks endocarditis: The patient does have a history of SLE, Libman-Sacks endocarditis typically presents with symptoms related to valve dysfunction, such as murmurs or signs of heart failure. questions.stem: Which of the following does not correspond to brainstem death?
questions.stemHtml: Which of the following does not correspond to brainstem death?
questions.solution: Correct Option C - Absence of toe jerk: Brain death is when functional brainstem death occurs permanently such that consciousness and spontaneous respiration are impossible . Certain preconditions have to be met for the diagnosis of brain death: The patient must have undergone severe brain damage of known cause Is highly unconscious and unresponsive Requires ventilation No known CNS depressants and muscle relaxants are causing the clinical presentation. Absence of low body temperature, severe hypotension and metabolic or hormonal pathologies With the satisfaction of preconditions, a formal assessment of the brainstem reflexes can be performed. These are to be performed by two clinicians not associated with the transplant team on two separate occasions. The absence of cranial reflexes, motor responses, and spontaneous respiration characterises brain death. An absence of a motor response to painful stimuli to the head/face or within the cranial nerve distribution to adequate stimulation of any somatic area indicates brainstem death. Spinal reflexes such as toe or finger movements do not indicate brainstem death. Incorrect Options: Option A - Absence of pupillary reflex: The absence of cranial nerve reflexes characterises brainstem death. These reflexes are: Pupillary Corneal Gag (pharyngeal) Tracheal (cough) Oculovestibular (caloric) Option B - Absence of spontaneous respiration: The absence of spontaneous respiration characterises brainstem death which is checked in the following manner: Pre Ventilation with 100% oxygen is given for a minimum of 5 minutes. Then, the patient is detached from the ventilator for 10 minutes to confirm the absence of respiration. During this time, the arterial PO 2 must be >8kPa (60 mmHg ) to ensure adequate respiratory stimulation. 6L/min oxygen is delivered through the endotracheal catheter to prevent hypoxia during the apnoea. Option D - Absence of cough: A cough or tracheal reflex is a cranial reflex which characterises brainstem death. @Neet_pg_bot
questions.solutionHtml:
Correct Option C - Absence of toe jerk:

  • Brain death is when functional brainstem death occurs permanently such that consciousness and spontaneous respiration are impossible.
  • Certain preconditions have to be met for the diagnosis of brain death:
    • The patient must have undergone severe brain damage of known cause
    • Is highly unconscious and unresponsive
    • Requires ventilation
    • No known CNS depressants and muscle relaxants are causing the clinical presentation.
    • Absence of low body temperature, severe hypotension and metabolic or hormonal pathologies
  • With the satisfaction of preconditions, a formal assessment of the brainstem reflexes can be performed.
  • These are to be performed by two clinicians not associated with the transplant team on two separate occasions.
  • The absence of cranial reflexes, motor responses, and spontaneous respiration characterises brain death.
  • An absence of a motor response to painful stimuli to the head/face or within the cranial nerve distribution to adequate stimulation of any somatic area indicates brainstem death.
  • Spinal reflexes such as toe or finger movements do not indicate brainstem death.

 

Incorrect Options:

Option A - Absence of pupillary reflex:

  • The absence of cranial nerve reflexes characterises brainstem death.
  • These reflexes are:
    • Pupillary
    • Corneal
    • Gag (pharyngeal)
    • Tracheal (cough)
    • Oculovestibular (caloric)

Option B - Absence of spontaneous respiration:

  • The absence of spontaneous respiration characterises brainstem death which is checked in the following manner:
    • Pre Ventilation with 100% oxygen is given for a minimum of 5 minutes. Then, the patient is detached from the ventilator for 10 minutes to confirm the absence of respiration.
    • During this time, the arterial PO2 must be >8kPa (60 mmHg) to ensure adequate respiratory stimulation.
    • 6L/min oxygen is delivered through the endotracheal catheter to prevent hypoxia during the apnoea.

Option D - Absence of cough:

  • A cough or tracheal reflex is a cranial reflex which characterises brainstem death.

questions.stemHtml: Following resection of a tumor of the anterior portion of the left temporal lobe, what defect would be expected?

options.label: C

questions.solution: Correct Option B - A homonymous right superior quadrantanopia: The left optic radiations serving vision in the right hemifield (in both eyes) originate in the left lateral geniculate nucleus and project to the primary visual cortex in the occipital lobe. Fibers serving the superior right quadrant of vision (in both eyes) project through the left temporal lobe in a structure known as the loop of Meyer which passes anteriorly as far as approximately 2.5 cm from the tip of the temporal lobe. Fibers serving the inferior right quadrant of vision (in both eyes) project through the parietal lobe to the primary visual cortex. Lesions of the optic tracts classically cause incongruous (asymmetric between the two eyes) field defects because the visual pathway fibers serving corresponding points in space are not closely approximated. In other words, the more posterior the lesion of the retrochiasmal visual pathways, the more organized the visual pathways fibers are and the more congruous (or symmetric) the visual field defects tend to be. Indeed, occipital lobe lesions tend to cause very congruous homonymous field defects. Lesions of the optic tract anterior to the brachium of the superior colliculus are expected to cause an incongruous contralateral homonymous hemianopic field defect AND a contralateral afferent pupillary defect. The afferent input to the pupillary light reflex, however, separates from the visual pathways just anterior to the lateral geniculate nucleus. Therefore, retrogeniculate optic pathway lesions AND pure lateral geniculate nucleus lesions (not involving the optic tract) do not affect pupillary function. Incorrect Options: Option A - A homonymous right inferior quadrantanopia: This option is incorrect because the lesion described in the question involves the anterior portion of the left temporal lobe. Lesions in this area would affect the fibers that carry visual information from the superior right quadrant of the visual field in both eyes. As a result, a homonymous right superior quadrantanopia would be expected, not an inferior quadrantanopia. Option C - A monocular right inferior quadrantanopia in the right eye only: Monocular field defects are not caused by lesions in the brain but rather by abnormalities in the eye itself or along the optic nerve. The lesion described in the question is located in the anterior portion of the left temporal lobe, which is a cerebral region. Therefore, monocular field defects would not be expected. Option D - A monocular right superior quadrantanopia in the right eye only: Similar to option C, monocular field defects are not caused by cerebral lesions. A lesion in the anterior portion of the left temporal lobe would not result in a monocular field defect in the right eye. Option E - A left afferent pupillary defect: Afferent pupillary defects (also known as a Marcus Gunn pupil) are typically caused by lesions affecting the optic nerve or severe retinal disease in the eye. The lesion described in the question is not located along the optic nerve, and it would not cause an afferent pupillary defect. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stemHtml: Which of the following is true regarding epidural injections for treatment of radicular pain?

options.label: A
options.text: Epidural injections are considered first line therapy for treatment of radicular pain and radiculopathy

options.label: B
options.text: There is better evidence supporting epidural injections as a therapeutic procedure in the cervical spine than in the lumbar spine

options.label: C
options.text: In the lumbar region, transforaminal injections are generally preferred over interlaminar and caudal epidural injections

options.label: D
options.text: A protocol of weekly injections for at least 3 weeks is recommended as most patients require multiple injections to demonstrate symptomatic benefit

questions.answerText: In the lumbar region, transforaminal injections are generally preferred over interlaminar and caudal epidural injections
questions.solution: Correct Option C - In the lumbar region, transforaminal injections are generally preferred over interlaminar and caudal epidural injections: Radicular pain is a common clinical problem, especially in the lumbar spine. Studies suggest that there is both a mechanical and an inflammatory component contributing to pain production in this condition which is basis for targeted injection of corticosteroids as a therapeutic modality. In the lumbar region, there is less evidence of benefit from interlaminar and caudal epidural injections compared to transforaminal injections which are preferred in this region. Interlaminar and caudal epidural injections can still be used if the transforaminal route is not feasible for example due to anatomic limitations. Incorrect Options: Option A - Epidural injections are considered first line therapy for treatment of radicular pain and radiculopathy: Conservative therapy is still considered the first line treatment for radicular pain. Epidural injections should be reserved for who have failed a trial of conservative treatment. Option B - There is better evidence supporting epidural injections as a therapeutic procedure in the cervical spine than in the lumbar spine: The evidence for epidural injections as a therapeutic procedure is much better for their use in the lumbar region than in the cervical or thoracic region. Option D - A protocol of weekly injections for at least 3 weeks is recommended as most patients require multiple injections to demonstrate symptomatic benefit: Scheduled frequent injections are not supported by literature and should not be routinely performed. A decision to repeat an injection should be based on an individual patient’s response. Option E - Possible complications of epidural injections include allergy to the medications, radiation exposure, dural puncture, needle injury to nerves and blood vessels and, rarely, spinal cord infarction. Risks of epidural injections are greater in the lumbar spine: Allergy to the medications, radiation exposure, dural puncture, needle injury to nerves and blood vessels and, rarely, spinal cord infarction are all potential complications of epidural injections. However, the risks are considered greater in the cervical spine. @Neet_pg_bot

options.label: A
options.text: Cladribine – broad-spectrum, cell-cycle nonspecific cytotoxic agent that affects B and T cells, suppressing humoral and cell-mediated immunity

options.label: B
options.text: Cyclophosphamide – purine nucleoside and antimetabolite that reduces lymphocyte subpopulations especially CD4 and CD8 cells

options.label: C
options.text: Mitoxantrone – partially humanized monoclonal antibody targeting CD20 leading to depletion of circulating B cells

questions.answerText: Alemtuzumab – humanized monoclonal antibody that leads to depletion of CD52-expressing cells
questions.solution: Correct Option D - Alemtuzumab – humanized monoclonal antibody that leads to depletion of CD52-expressing cells: Binding to CD52: Alemtuzumab binds specifically to the CD52 antigen present on the surface of lymphocytes, particularly T cells and B cells. CD52 is also expressed on other immune cells like monocytes, macrophages, and eosinophils. Cell Depletion: Once alemtuzumab binds to CD52, it triggers the immune system to recognize the lymphocytes (T cells, B cells, and other CD52-expressing cells) as foreign or abnormal. This recognition leads to the destruction and clearance of these cells from the bloodstream and tissues. Immunomodulation: By depleting the lymphocytes, alemtuzumab significantly reduces the population of immune cells responsible for mounting an immune response. This can help in dampening the immune system's activity and reducing the inflammation associated with autoimmune diseases. Immune Reconstitution: After the initial depletion of immune cells, the immune system begins to regenerate. The process of immune cell reconstitution involves the production of new lymphocytes from stem cells in the bone marrow. As new cells are generated, there is an opportunity for resetting the immune system's balance and potentially reducing autoimmune activity. questions.stem: A medical student in the beginning of 3rd year comes to your office with a complaint of excessive tiredness. She is having trouble concentrating and finds herself dozing off in lectures and during morning rounds. She has always been a “night owl”. In college, she took all afternoon classes so she could sleep in. She would go to bed at 2 AM and get up at 10 or 11 AM and had no trouble falling asleep or staying awake during the day. In the first 2 years of medical school, she skipped all morning lectures. However, as a third year, she has to be in the hospital no later than 7 AM to pre-round her patients. She tries to go to bed at 9:00 PM, but lies awake in bed until the middle of the night despite being “exhausted.” She has trouble getting up at 5:30 AM when her alarm goes off. On her days off, she goes to sleep when she’s tired, usually “pretty late,” falls asleep easily, and then sleeps in, sometimes until the afternoon. Her partner says she does not snore or wake up gasping. She has not experienced any episodes of muscle weakness or paralysis. She admits that she is stressed but not more than usual. She drinks socially but denies any illicit drug use. She drinks several cups of coffee throughout the morning but not after 2 PM Which of the following diagnostic tests could help confirm the most likely diagnosis?

questions.solution: Correct Option C - Actigraphy: This patient reports a chronic inability to fall asleep and wake up at socially acceptable times which is consistent with a circadian rhythm disorder. Her sleep and daytime function are normal when she is allowed to maintain a late bedtime and rise time which supports a diagnosis of delayed sleep-phase disorder (DSPD). Actigraphy is a device worn on the wrist which uses either an activity monitor or a motion detector to record movement. The absence of movement for a continuous period of time is suggestive of sleep, while sustained movement for a continuous period of time is suggestive of wakefulness. Actigraphy is used in conjunction with sleep diaries in suspected DSPD for objective confirmation of a pattern of delayed bedtime and rise time. Incorrect Options: Option A - Overnight polysomnogram: Overnight polysomnogram (PSG) is not indicated in the evaluation of DSPD unless another comorbid sleep disorder such as obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) is suspected. This patient has no symptoms to suggest comorbid OSA or any another sleep disorder that would be diagnosed through a PSG. Option B - Multiple sleep latency test: Multiple sleep latency testing consists of a series of daytime naps during which the latency to sleep and the presence of sleep-onset REM periods are recorded. It provides an objective measure of an individual’s tendency to fall asleep and is used in the evaluation of suspected narcolepsy and hypersomnia. Option D - Measurement of cerebral spinal fluid hypocretin level: Cerebral spinal fluid hypocretin levels can be useful in the evaluation of narcolepsy but have no role in the diagnostic work-up of circadian rhythm disorders. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.answerText: It is the most common of the trigeminal autonomic cephalalgias
questions.solution: Correct Option C - It is the most common of the trigeminal autonomic cephalalgias: The trigeminal autonomic cephalalgias (TACs) are a group of primary headache disorders that include short-lasting unilateral neuralgiform headache attacks with conjunctival injection and tearing (SUNCT), short-lasting unilateral neuralgiform headache attacks with cranial autonomic features (SUNA), paroxysmal hemicrania, hemicranias continua, and cluster headache. Of this group, cluster headache has the highest prevalence, affecting approximately 0.1% of the population (option C is correct). Incorrect Options: Option A - It affects women more than men: Cluster headache affects men approximately 3 times more than women (option A is incorrect). Option B - Unlike migraine, a genetic predisposition has not been suggested for cluster headaches: Recent evidence suggests there is a genetic predisposition with first-degree relatives of patients having 14-48 times the risk of the general population (option B is incorrect). Option D - The majority of patients have the chronic form: Most patients have the episodic form in which headache clusters are separated by remission periods of greater than 4 weeks (option D is incorrect). @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A 38-year-old female patient is intubated and admitted to the critical care unit after she suffered a traumatic brain injury as a result of a motorcycle accident. Intracranial pressure (ICP) per monitor is 36 mmHg. Fifty grams of mannitol is administered intravenously, and the patient is hyperventilated. Which of the following is correct regarding the treatment of elevated ICP?
questions.stemHtml: A 38-year-old female patient is intubated and admitted to the critical care unit after she suffered a traumatic brain injury as a result of a motorcycle accident. Intracranial pressure (ICP) per monitor is 36 mmHg. Fifty grams of mannitol is administered intravenously, and the patient is hyperventilated. Which of the following is correct regarding the treatment of elevated ICP?

options.label: B
options.text: Mannitol decreases serum osmolality, allowing flow down a gradient into the intravascular space.

options.label: C
options.text: Glucocorticoids should be implemented in patients with moderate to severe head injury.

options.label: D
options.text: Midline shift on computed tomography (CT) is the most sensitive early sign of increased intracranial pressure (ICP).

questions.solution: Correct Option A - Serum osmolarity should be > 280 mOsm/L: The skull has a fixed volume of 1400 to 1700 mL, which normally includes brain parenchyma (80%), cerebrospinal fluid (10%), and blood (10%). Intracranial pressure, normally ≤ 15 mmHg in adults, can be increased in association with trauma, mass lesions, obstruction of outflow from the central nervous system (CNS), hydrocephalus, and hepatic encephalopathy. Patients who have increased ICP should be monitored carefully and treated to reduce the ICP as well as the underlying cause. Although brain volume is usually stable, it can be increased by mass lesions. Obstruction of cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) outflow or pathologic increases in CSF production (normally 500 mL/day) can increase ICP. The volume of blood in the CNS can also be increased in patients with hypoxia or hypercapnia. Autoregulation may fail in patients with neurologic injury. Cerebral perfusion pressure is determined by subtracting intracranial pressure from mean arterial pressure. Decreases in cerebral perfusion pressure can result in ischemia, and increases may result in edema or hypertensive encephalopathy. Increased ICP typically results in headaches and changes in the level of consciousness, focal neurological symptoms, papilledema, and Cushing's reflex (hypertension, bradycardia, and respiratory depression). Blood pressure should be maintained to keep a cerebral perfusion pressure of 60 mmHg or higher. The mannitol therapy should be guided by 12 hourly measurements of serum osmolality. Mannitol should be used for 48 hours only if facilities for measuring serum osmolality are not available. Incorrect Options: Option B - Mannitol decreases serum osmolality, allowing flow down a gradient into the intravascular space: Mannitol actually increases serum osmolality, not decreases it. When mannitol is administered intravenously, it creates an osmotic gradient that draws free water from the brain parenchyma into the intravascular space. This osmotic diuretic effect reduces brain volume and helps to decrease intracranial pressure (ICP) in patients with elevated ICP. Option C - Glucocorticoids should be implemented in patients with moderate to severe head injury: The use of glucocorticoids, such as dexamethasone, is not recommended in patients with head trauma or traumatic brain injury. In fact, the use of glucocorticoids in this population has been associated with worse outcomes and increased mortality. Glucocorticoids may increase the risk of infection and delay wound healing, which can be detrimental in patients with traumatic brain injury. Option D - Midline shift on computed tomography (CT) is the most sensitive early sign of increased intracranial pressure (ICP): While midline shift on CT scan can be indicative of increased ICP, it is not the most sensitive early sign. Other early signs of increased ICP include headache, altered level of consciousness, pupillary changes (e.g., fixed and dilated pupils), and focal neurological deficits. Midline shift on CT scan is a later finding and may indicate significant mass effect from a lesion, such as a tumor or hematoma, causing compression of brain structures. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.solution: Correct Option D - Abdominal ultrasound: Abdominal ultrasound is not indicated in the routine evaluation for systemic sequelae of CPEO. On examination, there is no remarkable finding but laboratory investigations reveal a serum sodium level of 128mEq/L, serum osmolality 270mOsm/kg, urinary sodium level of 44mEq/L, and urinary osmolality 110mOsm/kg. questions.solution: Correct Option A - Fluid restriction: Syndrome of inappropriate ADH secretion (SIADH) is characterized by excess ADH secretion which causes excess water absorption from the kidney and results in concentrated urine SIADH is diagnosed by Serum sodium lower than 135mEq/L Serum osmolality lower than 275mOsm/kg Urine sodium higher than 40mEq/L Urine osmolality higher than 100mOsm/kg With normal blood pressure and euvolemia and no other causes of hyponatremia Pulmonary diseases like pneumonia, asthma, acute respiratory failure, and pneumothorax can cause SIADH due to unknown mechanism Clinical manifestations are due to decreased serum osmolality due to ADH-mediated water retention and secondary solute loss which causes cerebral edema The 1st line treatment for a patient with mild symptoms is the fluid restriction The daily water intake is restricted to less than 800ml only This restricted intake of water decreases free water in the body and increases serum osmolality and improves symptoms Incorrect Options: Option B - Salt tablets: If the 1st line treatment of water restriction is not helpful and hyponatremia is persistent then sodium chloride in the form of salt tablets can be given to correct hyponatremia Salt tablets cause effective and rapid response than water restriction Option C - Salt tablets with furosemide: Salt tablets (sodium chloride) can be used with furosemide (a loop diuretic) as it decreases the urine concentration and helps the excretion of water This is not a first-line treatment and is used after water restriction Option D - Hypertonic saline infusion: The hypertonic saline infusion will rapidly increase the serum sodium levels and will cause osmotic demyelination syndrome In a patient with mild symptoms of hyponatremia rapid correction with hypertonic saline is not recommended @Neet_pg_bot
questions.solutionHtml:
Correct Option A - Fluid restriction:

  • Syndrome of inappropriate ADH secretion (SIADH) is characterized by excess ADH secretion which causes excess water absorption from the kidney and results in concentrated urine
  • SIADH is diagnosed by
    • Serum sodium lower than 135mEq/L
    • Serum osmolality lower than 275mOsm/kg
    • Urine sodium higher than 40mEq/L
    • Urine osmolality higher than 100mOsm/kg
    • With normal blood pressure and euvolemia and no other causes of hyponatremia
  • Pulmonary diseases like pneumonia, asthma, acute respiratory failure, and pneumothorax can cause SIADH due to unknown mechanism
  • Clinical manifestations are due to decreased serum osmolality due to ADH-mediated water retention and secondary solute loss which causes cerebral edema
  • The 1st line treatment for a patient with mild symptoms is the fluid restriction
  • The daily water intake is restricted to less than 800ml only
  • This restricted intake of water decreases free water in the body and increases serum osmolality and improves symptoms

Incorrect Options:

Option B - Salt tablets:

  • If the 1st line treatment of water restriction is not helpful and hyponatremia is persistent then sodium chloride in the form of salt tablets can be given to correct hyponatremia
  • Salt tablets cause effective and rapid response than water restriction

Option C - Salt tablets with furosemide:

  • Salt tablets (sodium chloride) can be used with furosemide (a loop diuretic) as it decreases the urine concentration and helps the excretion of water
  • This is not a first-line treatment and is used after water restriction

Option D - Hypertonic saline infusion:

  • The hypertonic saline infusion will rapidly increase the serum sodium levels and will cause osmotic demyelination syndrome
  • In a patient with mild symptoms of hyponatremia rapid correction with hypertonic saline is not recommended

questions.stem: A second-year medical student learns about the regulation and function of prolactin in his endocrinology lecture. Which of the following dopaminergic pathway is involved in the secretion of prolactin?
questions.stemHtml: A second-year medical student learns about the regulation and function of prolactin in his endocrinology lecture. Which of the following dopaminergic pathway is involved in the secretion of prolactin?
questions.solution: Correct Option D - Tuberoinfundibular: Prolactin is secreted by the anterior pituitary gland . Its secretion is inhibited by the production of dopamine by the tuberoinfundibular pathway of the hypothalamus . Decreased activity of this pathway results in increased production of prolactin. Thyroid-releasing hormone (TRH) can also stimulate the production of prolactin in conditions like primary or secondary hypothyroidism. Prolactin can inhibit its own secretion by increasing dopamine production from the hypothalamus. Functions of prolactin include: Stimulation of milk production Inhibition of ovulation (females) Inhibition of spermatogenesis (males) Dopamine agonists (cabergoline) are used to treat conditions in which prolactin excess (prolactinoma). Drugs like antipsychotics and antidepressants can decrease dopamine production and can result in an increase in prolactin levels. Incorrect Options: Option A - Mesocortical: Decreased activity of the mesocortical pathway results in negative symptoms like anergia and apathy. It is affected minimally by antipsychotics. Option B - Mesolimbic: Increased activity of the mesolimbic pathway results in positive symptoms like delusions and hallucinations. Antipsychotics have a marked effect on these pathways. Option C - Nigrostriatal: Decreased activity of nigrostriatal pathways results in extrapyramidal symptoms like dystonia and parkinsonism. It is notably affected by movement disorders. @Neet_pg_bot

Correct Option D - Tuberoinfundibular:

  • Thyroid-releasing hormone (TRH) can also stimulate the production of prolactin in conditions like primary or secondary hypothyroidism.

questions.solution: Correct Option D - Aging: This patient presented with symptoms of acromegaly and laboratory investigations confirmed the diagnosis. questions.stem: A 21-year-old female presented with truncal obesity with a moon face and buffalo hump. On examination, purple striae and muscle wasting are present. An endocrinologist wants to investigate by determining the blood levels of hormones and electrolytes. What is suspected in this case of Cushing syndrome?
questions.stemHtml: A 21-year-old female presented with truncal obesity with a moon face and buffalo hump. On examination, purple striae and muscle wasting are present. An endocrinologist wants to investigate by determining the blood levels of hormones and electrolytes. What is suspected in this case of Cushing syndrome?
questions.solution: Correct Option A - High cortisol and low ACTH: Cushing syndrome involves the excess of all adrenal hormones. It is diagnosed by: Demonstration of high cortisol level Serum ACTH levels Dexamethasone suppression test Salivary cortisol 24-hour urinary-free cortisol Radiologic imaging. The outpatient initial screening test is 24-hour urinary-free cortisol. The best initial diagnostic test is an overnight dexamethasone suppression test followed by a 1 mg loading dose. To localise the lesion, a high-dose dexamethasone suppression test is carried out to differentiate between pituitary adenoma and ectopic source. If ACTH is low and cortisol is high, there is either an adrenal adenoma or exogenous glucocorticoid intake. However, if ACTH is high and cortisol is low, then there is either pituitary adenoma or an ectopic source that secretes ACTH, such as small cell cancer of the lung. If the cortisol levels are suppressed, followed by a high-dose dexamethasone suppression test, the cause is a pituitary adenoma. Contrarily, if no suppression has occurred, the cause is an ectopic source of ACTH. Incorrect Options: Option B - High cortisol and high ACTH: If ACTH is high and cortisol is also high, there is either pituitary adenoma (Cushing’s disease) or an ectopic source that secretes ACTH, such as small cell cancer of the lung. Option C - Hyperkalemia and hyponatremia: In Cushing syndrome, there is an excess aldosterone secretion that results in hypernatremia and hypokalemia. Option D - Decreased urinary free cortisol: Increased urinary-free cortisol is present in Cushing syndrome. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.solution: Correct Option C - Autoimmune destruction of the Adrenal gland: PRIMARY ADRENAL INSUFFICIENCY (ADDISON’S DISEASE) Aetiology Autoimmune Infectious causes [Tuberculosis (most common), HIV, fungal] Hemorrhagic insult Metastatic disease Clinical features Weakness, weight loss, anorexia, fatigue, salt craving Gastrointestinal symptoms (vomiting, diarrhoea, and severe abdominal pain resembling peritonitis) Fever Postural hypotension Hyperpigmentation Hyperkalemia and hyponatremia Acute Adrenal crisis (shock, fever, altered mentation, abdominal pain) Diagnosis Serum ACTH, Serum cortisol, and high-dose ACTH stimulation test Primary Adrenal insufficiency: High ACTH and low cortisol Secondary Adrenal insufficiency: Low cortisol, low ACTH The patient presents with fatigue, recurrent abdominal pain, nausea, weight loss, hypotension, hyperpigmentation, and history of alopecia areata. Laboratory investigations show hyponatremia and hyperkalemia with low serum cortisol levels (even with corticotropin stimulation test). All these findings suggest a diagnosis of Addison’s disease. Up to 90% of primary Adrenal insufficiency in the Western world is caused by autoimmune adrenalitis. Other autoimmune diseases like alopecia areata, type 1 diabetes, vitiligo, pernicious anaemia, and chronic autoimmune thyroiditis are frequently linked to autoimmune adrenalitis. Incorrect Options: Option A - Haemorrhage within the Adrenal gland: An uncommon cause of primary Adrenal insufficiency is adrenal gland haemorrhage, which is frequently brought on by sepsis or prolonged anticoagulant medication. Since Adrenal haemorrhage typically affects critically sick patients with back or abdominal discomfort, the clinical presentation is acute (Adrenal crisis). Hyperpigmentation, among other clinical signs connected to chronic Adrenal insufficiency, would be exceptional. Option B - Destruction of the pituitary gland: Secondary Adrenal insufficiency is caused by the destruction of ACTH-producing pituitary cells by pituitary or parasellar tumours and pituitary infiltration (such as lymphocytic histiocytosis). Electrolyte abnormalities and skin darkening in this patient do not support secondary Adrenal insufficiency. The cortisol levels are low in secondary Adrenal insufficiency, but increase with corticotropin stimulation test, unlike in this patient. Hence, it is an unlikely cause of this patient’s presentation. Option D - Granulomatous infection of the Adrenal gland: In underdeveloped countries, Mycobacterium tuberculosis is the most frequent cause of granulomatous inflammation of the adrenal gland, a prevalent cause of primary Adrenal insufficiency. This patient neither has any known history of travelling where Tuberculosis is prevalent nor does he have any other risk factors for the disease. Primary Adrenal insufficiency can result from sarcoidosis, similarly, characterised by granulomatous inflammation. Alopecia areata, tiredness, and weight loss are additional effects of sarcoidosis. Sarcoidosis, however, is a very uncommon cause of primary Adrenal insufficiency. @Neet_pg_bot

She also reports episodes of palpitations and sweating for the last 10 days. Which of the following is least likely to be associated with this patient’s condition?

She also reports episodes of palpitations and sweating for the last 10 days. Which of the following is least likely to be associated with this patient’s condition?
questions.solution: Correct Option D - MEN 1 syndrome: This patient's history and present symptoms suggest the diagnosis of pheochromocytoma . Pheochromocytoma is a benign tumour of the adrenal gland. The tumour is composed of chromaffin cells. It releases hormones like epinephrine and norepinephrine. Signs and symptoms of pheochromocytoma include elevated blood pressure, headaches, sweating, palpitations, tremors, dyspnea, and weight loss. These symptoms of pheochromocytoma occur continuously or episodically. Certain activities or conditions such as exercise, stress, surgery, consuming foods containing high amounts of tyramine, and drugs (phenelzine) can trigger episodes of pheochromocytoma symptoms. Pheochromocytoma is associated with certain genetic disorders. These disorders involve the following: Multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2 (MEN 2) Von Hippel-Lindau disease (VHL) Neurofibromatosis 1 (NF1) Hereditary paraganglioma syndrome MEN 1 syndrome consists of pituitary tumours, hyperparathyroidism, and pancreatic neuroendocrine tumours (PNETs). Pheochromocytomas are not a part of MEN 1 syndrome. Incorrect Options: Option A - Von Hippel-Lindau (VHL) disease: VHL involves tumours of the CNS, pancreatic carcinoma, renal tumours, and endocrine cancers along with pheochromocytomas. Option B - Neurofibromatosis 1 (NF1): NF1 consists of skin cancers, optic nerve tumours, pigmented lesions of the skin and pheochromocytomas. Option C - Multiple endocrine neoplasia 2 (MEN 2) syndrome: There are two types of MEN 2 syndromes, type 2A and type 2B. The condition is associated with multiple thyroid, parathyroid, and digestive tumours along with pheochromocytomas. @Neet_pg_bot
